properties.question: In one sentence, what does the protocol do, for whom, and what does the receiving service get from it?
Where is it used and between whom? At which layer (HTTP header, token, message body)? Who can verify it (the service itself, a CDN, a gateway)?
Which parties does the spec define, and what does each do? Use the spec's own names and its "Roles", "Participants" or "Terminology" section.

What is the formal status (RFC, current dated revision, working-group draft, individual draft, vendor specification)? Latest version and date? Who maintains it? Which named products send or verify it?
Which standards does it build on (with RFC numbers)? Note non-standard dependencies (vendor programmes) and deprecated parts.
What does the agent identifier look like, and what does it actually name (client application, agent provider, the provider's key or URL, a domain, the individual agent)?
Can the service tell which specific agent instance sent the request, not just which application or provider?
Does the service learn whom the agent is acting for (user, consumer, organisation)? Is this required, optional, or only possible through another party?

What credential does the service receive on each request (bearer token, HTTP Message Signature, mTLS certificate, verifiable credential)? What exactly is signed or bound (host, path, time, nonce, body)? Is it proof of possession?
How long is the credential valid? Is the limit a MUST, a SHOULD or unspecified? Is the verifier told to reject longer ones?
Can the service check that the credential is genuine, current and unaltered, without a prior relationship with the agent? What does it check, and against what?

properties.property: Authentication of the agent or user
properties.question: Does the receiving service itself authenticate the party making the request (the individual agent or the user)? Who exactly is authenticated, and by whom?
Does the protocol tell the service what the agent is allowed to do (scopes, per-action limits)? How fine-grained is it?
Does the protocol include a step where a person approves the agent's access or action? Can the service ask for it?
Once the credential is valid, why should the service rely on the party behind it? Who vouches for the agent (a central authority, the authorization server and the user's consent, a registry, nobody)?
Does the protocol define a way to revoke an agent's access? Who can revoke what, how fast does it take effect at the service, and at what granularity (one instance, one user, a whole provider)?
Can the service contact whoever is responsible for the agent (agent provider, user, model provider) if something goes wrong? Is a contact field required, optional or absent?
Can one service warn others about a misbehaving agent (shared signals, reputation, abuse reports)?
Does the service learn which AI model (and version) is behind the agent? Is it verifiable or self-asserted?

protocol.name: A2A
protocol.spec_version: A2A Protocol v1.0.1 (git tag v1.0.1, commit 3303592)
protocol.maintainer: A2A project under the Linux Foundation (contributed by Google), guided by a technical steering committee
protocol.newer_version_note: v1.0.1 is the latest released version. A release candidate v1.1.0-rc (tagged 2026-10-29) exists and was not analysed; it adds, among other things, a section stating that A2A does not define the scope, validity or revocation of in-task authorization.

summary: The Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol is an open standard for AI agents built by different vendors and frameworks to discover each other, hand over tasks and exchange results, without sharing their internal memory or tools. One agent (the A2A client) sends messages and tasks to another agent (the A2A server, or remote agent), which publishes an Agent Card describing what it can do and how callers must authenticate. Google started the project in April 2025; it is now maintained under the Linux Foundation. Version 1.0 was released in March 2026 as the first stable version, and v1.0.1 (May 2026) is the latest release. Microsoft Foundry Agent Service, among others, serves it.

For identity and access, A2A deliberately reuses standard web security rather than defining its own. The server lists in its Agent Card which schemes it accepts (API key, HTTP authentication such as a bearer token, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect or mutual TLS); the client obtains credentials outside A2A and sends them with every request, and the server must authenticate and authorize every request. A2A messages themselves carry no user or client identity. Agent Cards can be signed, which helps the client trust the server, not the other way round. A2A defines a task state for asking the client to obtain extra authorization mid-task, but no client agent identifier, credential lifetime, revocation, contact channel or model identity.
how_it_works: The A2A server (the receiving agent) publishes an Agent Card, e.g. at /.well-known/agent-card.json, describing its skills, endpoints and the security schemes and scopes it requires. The card may be signed with JWS.
The A2A client (the calling agent or application) reads the Agent Card and picks a protocol binding (JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON) and a security scheme.
The client obtains the matching credential outside A2A, e.g. an OAuth access token from the authorization server named in the card, an API key, or a client certificate for mutual TLS.
The client sends a message (e.g. SendMessage) with the credential in an HTTP header or gRPC metadata on every request. A2A messages carry no user or client identity of their own.

The server authenticates the request with its declared scheme, applies its own authorization policy (e.g. per-skill scopes), and creates or continues a task. If it needs more authorization during the task, it sets the task to TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED and the client arranges it outside A2A.

rows.short: Agents delegate tasks to other agents
rows.answer: An open protocol in which one AI agent sends tasks and messages to another agent's A2A endpoint, discovered through that agent's Agent Card, with authentication delegated to standard web schemes (API keys, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, mutual TLS) that the receiving agent declares.

claims.text: A2A is an open standard for communication between independent agent systems.
claims.quote: The Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol is an open standard designed to facilitate communication and interoperability between independent, potentially opaque AI agent systems.

claims.text: Every A2A server publishes an Agent Card.
claims.quote: A2A Servers MUST make an Agent Card available.

claims.text: Authentication schemes are declared in the Agent Card and credentials are obtained outside A2A.
claims.quote: The client discovers the server's required authentication schemes via the securitySchemes field in the AgentCard.

rows.short: Agent-to-agent task delegation over HTTP or gRPC
rows.answer: Multi-agent systems where an agent or application (the A2A client) delegates work to a remote agent (the A2A server), across vendors and organisations. Messages travel in the body of JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP+JSON requests; credentials travel in HTTP headers or gRPC metadata, and identity is established at that transport layer, not inside A2A messages. The receiving agent, or a gateway in front of it, verifies the credential with whatever scheme it declared.

claims.text: The client initiates requests on behalf of a user or another system.
claims.quote: A2A Client: An application or agent that initiates requests to an A2A Server on behalf of a user or another system.

claims.text: Three standard protocol bindings.
claims.quote: Layer 3: Protocol Bindings provides concrete mappings of the abstract operations and data structures to specific protocol bindings (JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP/REST)

claims.text: Credentials are sent in headers or metadata on every request.
claims.quote: The client includes these credentials in protocol-appropriate headers or metadata for every A2A request.

claims.text: Identity is handled at the transport layer, not inside A2A.
claims.quote: Identity information is handled at the protocol layer, not within A2A semantics.

claims.text: Verification by a gateway in front of the agent is not described by A2A; it follows from the use of standard HTTP authentication schemes (inference).
claims.quote: A2A delegates authentication to standard web mechanisms.

rows.short: A2A client, A2A server (remote agent), user
rows.answer: A2A Client: an application or agent that starts requests to an A2A server on behalf of a user or another system. A2A Server (Remote Agent): an agent that exposes an A2A endpoint, processes tasks and publishes an Agent Card naming its provider (organization and URL). User: the party the client acts for; messages from the client side carry the role "user". Credential issuers (e.g. an OAuth authorization server or OpenID Connect provider) and agent registries appear only by reference; A2A does not define them as roles.

claims.text: A2A Client role.
claims.quote: A2A Client: An application or agent that initiates requests to an A2A Server on behalf of a user or another system.

claims.text: A2A Server role.
claims.quote: A2A Server (Remote Agent): An agent or agentic system that exposes an A2A-compliant endpoint, processing tasks and providing responses.

claims.text: The Agent Card names the server's provider.
claims.quote: The name of the agent provider's organization.

claims.text: The client-side message role is called user.
claims.quote: The message is from the client to the server.

claims.text: Registries are a discovery option without a defined API.
claims.quote: The current A2A specification does not prescribe a standard API for curated registries.

rows.short: HTTP, JSON-RPC, gRPC, OpenAPI security schemes, OAuth, JWS
rows.answer: Transport: HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC and Server-Sent Events, with Protocol Buffers as the normative data model. Security schemes follow the OpenAPI 3.2 Security Scheme Object: API key, HTTP authentication, OAuth 2.0 (with RFC 8414 metadata, PKCE and the device code flow), OpenID Connect and mutual TLS; the OAuth implicit and password flows are deprecated. Agent Card signing uses JWS (RFC 7515) over JSON canonicalized with JCS (RFC 8785).

claims.text: Reuses HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0 and SSE.
claims.quote: Reuse existing, well-understood standards (HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0, Server-Sent Events).

claims.text: Security schemes are based on OpenAPI 3.2.
claims.quote: This is a discriminated union type based on the OpenAPI 3.2 Security Scheme Object.

claims.text: Implicit flow deprecated in favour of authorization code with PKCE.
claims.quote: Deprecated: Use Authorization Code + PKCE instead.

claims.text: Agent Card signing uses JWS.
claims.quote: Agent Cards MAY be digitally signed using JSON Web Signature (JWS) as defined in RFC 7515 to ensure authenticity and integrity.

claims.text: Canonicalization uses JCS (RFC 8785).
claims.quote: Before signing, the Agent Card content MUST be canonicalized using the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined in RFC 8785.

rows.answer: No A2A identifier for the calling agent. The Agent Card identifies the receiving agent (the server) to the caller, not the other way round, and A2A messages carry no client or user identity. Whatever identity the server learns comes from the security scheme it chose (e.g. an API key, an OAuth token's client, or a client certificate), so its form and meaning are left to that scheme.
rows.rating_reason: Red: A2A defines no identifier for the agent side; identity comes only from the external credential scheme. This differs from MCP Authorization (yellow), which requires a client_id from its own registration mechanisms.

claims.text: The Agent Card describes the server, not the client.
claims.quote: The Agent Card describes the server's identity, capabilities, skills, and interaction requirements.

claims.text: A2A payloads carry no user or client identity.
claims.quote: A2A protocol payloads, such as JSON-RPC messages, don't carry user or client identity information directly.

claims.text: Identity is established at the transport layer.
claims.quote: Identity is established at the transport/HTTP layer.

claims.text: Searched Core Concepts, the Message object, Section 7 and the proto for a client or caller identifier. The Message has only a message ID, a role and optional context and task IDs.

rows.answer: No. A2A defines no identifier for a specific calling agent instance. The contextId and taskId fields group related messages and track units of work; they identify a conversation or a task, not the agent that sent it, and the server usually generates them. The tenant field routes requests to one of several agents behind a server endpoint, so it names a receiving agent, not a caller.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no per-instance identifier for the caller is defined (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.text: contextId groups related tasks and messages.
claims.quote: A contextId is an identifier that logically groups multiple related Task and Message objects, providing continuity across a series of interactions.

claims.text: Task IDs are generated by the server.
claims.quote: Task IDs are server-generated when a new task is created in response to a Message

claims.text: tenant routes to a receiving agent behind a shared endpoint.
claims.quote: An opaque string used for routing requests to a specific agent

claims.text: Searched Section 3.4, Section 7 and the proto Message and request objects for an agent instance or session identifier of the caller. None is defined.

rows.short: No; depends on chosen auth scheme
rows.answer: Not by A2A. The client acts on behalf of a user or another system, but A2A messages do not say who that is; the role "user" only marks a message as coming from the client side. The server may learn the user from its chosen credential (e.g. an OpenID Connect or OAuth token that represents an end user), and the documentation says authorization should use that identity, which could be a user, a client application, or both.
rows.rating_reason: Red: A2A defines no field naming the principal; it is available only if the external credential scheme carries it (native-only rule, same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: The client acts on behalf of a user or another system.
claims.quote: A2A Client: An application or agent that initiates requests to an A2A Server on behalf of a user or another system.

claims.text: Payloads carry no user identity.
claims.quote: A2A protocol payloads, such as JSON-RPC messages, don't carry user or client identity information directly.

claims.text: The authenticated identity could be a user, a client application, or both.
claims.quote: Authorization should be applied based on the authenticated identity, which could represent an end user, a client application, or both.

claims.text: The user role only marks the message direction.
claims.quote: The message is from the client to the server.

rows.short: Server's choice: API key, token, OAuth, OIDC, mTLS
rows.answer: Yes, a credential on every request, of a type the server chooses. The Agent Card declares one or more security schemes (API key, HTTP authentication such as a bearer token, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, or mutual TLS); the client sends the credential in headers or gRPC metadata on every request, and the server must authenticate each one. Except for mutual TLS, these are bearer credentials: whoever holds them can use them. For credentials passed in-band during a task, the spec recommends binding them to the requesting agent but defines no mechanism.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a credential declared by the server is presented on every request and must be verified (same as MCP Authorization); the answer notes most schemes are bearer credentials.

claims.text: Credentials are sent on every request.
claims.quote: The client includes these credentials in protocol-appropriate headers or metadata for every A2A request.

claims.text: The server must authenticate every request.
claims.quote: MUST authenticate every incoming request based on the provided credentials and its declared authentication requirements.

claims.text: Five scheme types are defined.
claims.quote: This is a discriminated union type based on the OpenAPI 3.2 Security Scheme Object.

claims.text: In-band credentials should be bound to the requesting agent, without a defined mechanism.
claims.quote: Credentials SHOULD be bound to the agent which originated the request, such that only this agent is able to use the credentials.

claims.text: Proof of possession: only the mutual TLS scheme proves possession of a key; API keys and bearer tokens are bearer credentials (inference from the scheme list; A2A defines no DPoP or similar binding).
claims.quote: A hint to the client to identify how the bearer token is formatted (e.g., "JWT").

rows.answer: Not specified. A2A sets no lifetime for the credentials sent with requests; that is left to the chosen scheme and its issuer (e.g. an OAuth authorization server). The security considerations only say credentials should be rotated periodically, which concerns replacing long-lived secrets, not how long each credential is accepted.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no lifetime is specified (MCP Authorization and Web Bot Auth at least recommend one, so they are yellow).

claims.text: Only periodic rotation is recommended.
claims.quote: Credentials SHOULD be rotated periodically

claims.text: Searched Sections 7, 13 and the security scheme objects for lifetime, expiry, short-lived or freshness rules for request credentials. None is set.

rows.short: Must reject invalid; checks left to scheme
rows.answer: Partly. The server must reject requests with missing or invalid credentials, but A2A does not say what makes a credential valid: it lists no checks for expiry, audience or signature. Those come from the chosen scheme; with OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect the card points to the issuer's metadata, so the server can validate tokens against it, while API keys and HTTP Basic credentials only work after the server has issued them to the client beforehand.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: rejection of invalid credentials is required, but A2A defines no validation steps and some schemes need prior setup with the client; lower of two plausible colours (the calibration examples define their checks and are green).

claims.text: Invalid credentials must be rejected.
claims.quote: Servers MUST reject requests with invalid or missing authentication credentials

claims.text: Credentials are obtained outside A2A.
claims.quote: The client obtains the necessary credentials through an out-of-band process specific to the required authentication scheme.

claims.text: The OAuth scheme can point to the authorization server's metadata.
claims.quote: URL to the OAuth2 authorization server metadata

claims.text: Searched Sections 3.3.2, 7 and 13 for required checks on expiry, audience, issuer or signature of request credentials. None is listed.
claims.section: 3.3.2. Error Handling; 7. Authentication and Authorization; 13. Security Considerations

rows.property: Authentication of the agent or user
rows.short: Credential check only; scheme decides whose
rows.answer: Not of the individual agent, as defined by A2A. The server must authenticate every request, but in A2A this means checking the credential of whichever scheme it declared; the credential is obtained outside A2A, and user sign-in, if any, happens at an OAuth or OpenID Connect provider. A2A defines no per-agent key, so a server learns the individual agent only if its own setup issues one (e.g. a client certificate per agent for mutual TLS).
rows.rating_reason: Red: the server checks a credential issued or set up outside A2A and no per-agent proof is defined (same as all three calibration examples), even though A2A requires the check itself.

claims.text: The server must authenticate every request against its declared requirements.
claims.quote: MUST authenticate every incoming request based on the provided credentials and its declared authentication requirements.

claims.text: Credentials come from an out-of-band process.
claims.quote: The client obtains the necessary credentials through an out-of-band process specific to the required authentication scheme.

claims.text: Credentials such as OAuth tokens or API keys come from processes outside A2A.
claims.quote: The A2A Client obtains the necessary credentials, such as OAuth 2.0 tokens or API keys, through processes external to the A2A protocol itself.

claims.text: The mutual TLS scheme carries only a description, so A2A does not say whose certificate it is (inference).
claims.quote: Defines a security scheme using mTLS authentication.

rows.short: Checks required; scopes optional, per skill
rows.answer: Partly. The server must run an authorization check on every request and limit results to what the caller may see, but the authorization model is the agent's own and is not prescribed by A2A. The Agent Card can state required OAuth scopes for the whole agent and for each skill, and the server may use scopes when deciding; this applies only when an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect scheme is used. A2A defines no per-action limits such as amounts.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: scopes are defined but only for OAuth-based schemes and the server only MAY consider them, while the authorization model is left to each agent; MCP Authorization is green because scopes are part of its normal flow.

claims.text: Authorization checks are required on every request.
claims.quote: Servers MUST implement authorization checks on every A2A Protocol Operations request

claims.text: The authorization model is not prescribed.
claims.quote: Authorization boundaries are defined by each agent's authorization model, not prescribed by the protocol

claims.text: Authorization logic may consider skills and OAuth scopes.
claims.quote: Authorization logic is implementation-specific and MAY consider:

claims.text: Each skill can declare its own security requirements.
claims.quote: Security schemes necessary for this skill.

claims.text: Security requirements map schemes to required scopes.
claims.quote: A map of security schemes to the required scopes.

rows.short: Optional mid-task request; approval outside A2A
rows.answer: Partly. During a task, the server can set the task to TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED to ask the client to obtain authorization, and the spec gives human approval before a destructive action as an example. The approval itself happens outside A2A: the client may pass the request to a person, another agent or a service, and credentials are delivered out of band. A user approval step in an OAuth flow, if used, also happens outside A2A.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a defined but optional way for the service to request approval, which may be fulfilled by software rather than a person; MCP Authorization is green because user approval is part of its main flow.

claims.text: Human approval is an example of in-task authorization.
claims.quote: An agent requiring human approval before a destructive action is taken

claims.text: The server can delegate the request to the client through a task state.
claims.quote: A2A provides the capability for agents to delegate the fulfillment of this authorization to the client via the TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED Task state.

claims.text: The client may hand the request to another human, agent or service.
claims.quote: Contact another human, agent, or service to fulfill the authorization request

claims.text: Credentials arrive out of band unless otherwise negotiated.
claims.quote: Agents MUST arrange to receive credentials via an out-of-band means, unless an in-band mechanism has been negotiated out-of-band or via an extension.

rows.short: Only the issuer named in OAuth/OIDC schemes
rows.answer: Partly. The server chooses its schemes, and for OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect the Agent Card points to the issuer, so a valid token means that issuer approved the client. For API keys and HTTP authentication the server is its own issuer, and the mutual TLS scheme names no certificate authority. Signed Agent Cards and registries help the client trust the server, not the server trust the client.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a vouching party is named only in some schemes; MCP Authorization is green because clients must use tokens from the server's named authorization server.

claims.text: The OIDC scheme names the provider's discovery URL.
claims.quote: The OpenID Connect Discovery URL for the OIDC provider's metadata.

claims.text: The OAuth scheme can name the authorization server's metadata.
claims.quote: URL to the OAuth2 authorization server metadata

claims.text: Agent Card signatures let clients verify the server's card.
claims.quote: Signatures allow clients to verify that an Agent Card has not been tampered with and originates from the claimed provider.

claims.text: The mutual TLS scheme object has only a description field and names no trust anchor (searched the proto and Section 7).

rows.answer: Not defined by A2A. The security considerations say agents should implement credential revocation mechanisms, but A2A defines none, so revocation depends on the chosen scheme: the server can delete an API key it issued, or the OAuth authorization server can revoke tokens (e.g. under RFC 7009), with the speed and granularity that scheme allows. The revocation rule for signing keys covers Agent Card signatures, which the client checks, not request credentials.
rows.rating_reason: Red: A2A only recommends (SHOULD) that agents have revocation and defines no mechanism, so coverage is none (same colour as all three calibration examples, which also leave revocation to other parties).

claims.text: Revocation mechanisms are recommended.
claims.quote: Agents SHOULD implement credential revocation mechanisms

claims.text: The only other revocation rule covers Agent Card signing keys, checked by clients.
claims.quote: Expired or revoked keys MUST NOT be used for verification

claims.text: Searched Sections 7, 13 and the proto for a revocation endpoint, status list or signal. None is defined.

rows.answer: No. The Agent Card names the provider organization and a URL, but that card describes the receiving agent and is read by the caller; the calling agent sends no card or contact details to the server. A2A defines no contact, abuse or security channel for whoever operates a calling agent.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no contact for the caller is defined (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.text: Provider details are part of the server's Agent Card.
claims.quote: A URL for the agent provider's website or relevant documentation.

claims.text: The Agent Card describes the server.
claims.quote: The Agent Card describes the server's identity, capabilities, skills, and interaction requirements.

claims.text: Searched the request objects, Section 7 and Section 13 for a caller contact, abuse or security field. None is defined.

rows.answer: No. A2A asks agents to log security events, watch for unusual patterns and rate-limit callers, but these are local measures. It defines no way for one agent to warn other agents, registries or credential issuers about a misbehaving caller.
rows.rating_reason: Red: not addressed (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.text: Security event logging is local.
claims.quote: Agents SHOULD log security-relevant events (authentication failures, authorization denials, suspicious requests)

claims.text: Searched Section 13, the discovery guide and the extension list for shared signals, reputation or abuse reporting. None is defined.

rows.answer: No. A2A says nothing about which AI model is behind the calling agent. The Agent Card's version field gives the version of the receiving agent, not a model, and the calling agent sends no card. Agents are treated as opaque by design.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no model identity (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.text: Agents are opaque by design.
claims.quote: Agents collaborate based on declared capabilities and exchanged information, without needing to share their internal thoughts, plans, or tool implementations.

goals_reading.access_control: The receiving agent must authenticate and authorize every request with the scheme it declared, and can require OAuth scopes per skill, but what is checked and how finely is left to each agent and to the external credential issuer.
goals_reading.incident_response: A2A defines no revocation; a misbehaving caller can be cut off only through the credential scheme (e.g. deleting its API key or revoking its OAuth grant), at the granularity that scheme gives, which is usually a client or user, not an agent instance.
goals_reading.accountability: An action can be traced only to whatever identity the credential carries (a key holder, an OAuth client, a user or a certificate subject); A2A messages add no caller, user or model identity.

notes: A2A is analysed from the side of the A2A server (the receiving agent). Many A2A identity features, such as the Agent Card and its signatures, help the calling agent trust the server, not the reverse; the rows say so where relevant.
A2A uses RFC 2119 keywords. The human approval row rests on lowercase wording ("provides the capability", "may"), so its requirement is marked MAY*.

Two rows also cite the A2A documentation page Enterprise Implementation of A2A, which is non-normative; it is used only where it repeats or explains the specification (e.g. that A2A payloads carry no user or client identity).
The specification file at the v1.0.1 tag still shows "Latest Released Version 1.0.0" in its header; the changelog dates v1.0.1 to 2026-05-26 and the git tag to 2026-05-28.
A Secure Passport extension is listed among example extensions in the A2A documentation; it lives in the samples repository, is not part of the specification and was not counted.
The Microsoft Learn page could not be checked by the script; its quote was checked with a web tool.
open_questions: Section 7.4 requires the server to authenticate every request. Does the project intend this to identify the calling agent, or only to validate the credential of the declared scheme?
The mutual TLS scheme object carries only a description. How is a server expected to tell clients which certificate authorities or certificates it accepts?
The v1.0.1 sample Agent Card uses a "security" field while the normative proto names it security_requirements (the v1.1.0 release candidate updates the sample). Implementations may differ on this.
Section 7.6.3 recommends binding in-band credentials to the requesting agent but gives no mechanism. Is an official extension planned for this?

protocol.name: AAuth
protocol.spec_version: draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11
protocol.maintainer: Dick Hardt (Hellō); an OpenID Foundation AAuth working group was created in November 2026

summary: AAuth is a proposed protocol that gives every AI agent its own cryptographic identity and lets it act for a person across organisations without being registered in advance at each service. It starts from the view that OAuth client IDs and API keys do not fit agents, which discover services at run time and work on long tasks across many organisations. It was written by Dick Hardt (Hellō) as an individual IETF draft, currently at revision -11 (September 2026). In November 2026 an OpenID Foundation working group was created to take it forward. Implementations so far are exploratory.

Each agent gets an identifier and an agent token from its agent provider and signs every request with its own key, so no token works without that key. On top of this, resources choose one of five access modes: recognising the agent alone, running their own sign-in, or relying on a person server that the person chooses. The person server tells the resource who the agent acts for (as a per-resource pseudonym), collects consent, and issues scoped auth tokens, optionally through the resource's own access server. It also supports missions, permission requests and audit records for governing agents, and a revocation cascade. AAuth does not define model identity, a contact channel or a trust registry, and in the person-based modes the resource does not see which agent it is talking to.
how_it_works: The agent creates a key pair and proves itself to its agent provider, which issues an agent token with the agent's identifier (aauth:local@domain) and public key.

The agent calls a resource with an HTTP Message Signature over the request and its agent token in the Signature-Key header. The resource checks the signature and the token, and may decide on the agent's identity alone.
If the resource needs to know the person, it asks for a person token. The agent gets one from its person server, which identifies the person to that resource with a pseudonymous identifier.

If the resource needs authorization, it returns a resource token describing the access it offers. The agent takes this to its person server, which collects the person's consent if needed (and, for four-party access, asks the resource's access server) and returns a scoped auth token.

The agent presents the auth token on its signed requests, and the resource enforces the scopes. Tokens last at most an hour and can be revoked through a cascade that starts at the agent provider or person server.

rows.short: Per-agent signed requests, plus person-based authorization
rows.answer: An IETF individual draft, now adopted by an OpenID Foundation working group, in which every agent has its own identifier and key and signs every request, and a person server it chooses can identify the person and grant scoped access.

rows.answer: Agents that call APIs and services on behalf of people or organisations, especially across organisational boundaries where the agent cannot be registered in advance. Identity and authorization travel in signed HTTP headers. A resource can choose among five access modes, from simply recognising the agent to full authorization through the person's server and its own access server, and can use different modes for different endpoints.

rows.short: Agent, agent provider, resource, person server, access server, person
rows.answer: Agent: an HTTP client acting for a person. Agent provider: issues each agent its identity and agent token. Resource: the API or service being called. Person server: chosen by the person; represents them, handles consent and missions, and issues person and auth tokens. Access server: optional policy engine for a resource. Person: the user or organisation accountable for the agent. A supervisor (the person, or a supervision server) makes approval decisions.

claims.quote: A user or organization — the legal person — on whose behalf an agent acts and who is accountable for the agent's actions.

claims.text: Access server.

claims.text: Supervisor.

In November 2026 an OpenID Foundation working group was created for AAuth, and specification work will move there. The listed implementations (TypeScript, .NET, Python, a Keycloak extension) are all marked exploratory; no production deployments are named.

rows.short: RFC 9421, HTTP Signature Keys, JWT, OpenID Connect
rows.answer: HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) for signing every request, with keys conveyed in the Signature-Key header defined in a companion draft (HTTP Signature Keys); JWTs (RFC 7519) for all tokens, bound to the agent's key with a confirmation claim (RFC 7800); well-known metadata and JWKS for key discovery (RFC 8615); and OpenID Connect scopes, claims and enterprise extensions. Companion drafts cover agent bootstrap, events and per-call authorization.

claims.quote: All requests are signed with HTTP Message Signatures

claims.text: JWT tokens verified through issuer metadata.

claims.text: OpenID Connect vocabulary.
claims.quote: AAuth reuses OpenID Connect scope values, identity claims, and enterprise extensions

rows.answer: Yes. The agent provider gives each agent its own identifier of the form aauth:local@domain, where the domain is the provider's. It names a specific agent with its own signing key, not just the application, and stays the same when the key rotates. The resource sees this identifier only in the two simplest access modes; in the person-based modes it is deliberately hidden (see the next row).
rows.rating_reason: Green: the identifier names the individual agent, unlike the client or provider identifiers of MCP Authorization, Web Bot Auth and Visa TAP.

claims.text: Identifier format.
claims.quote: An AP assigns each agent an identifier: a URI using the aauth scheme, of the form aauth:local@domain, where domain is the AP's domain.

claims.text: Per-instance by design.
claims.quote: AAuth's aauth:local@domain agent identifier identifies a specific instance with its own signing key.

claims.text: Stable across key rotation.
claims.quote: An agent identifier is stable across key rotations.

rows.short: Yes, but hidden in person-based modes
rows.answer: Partly. Each agent instance has its own identifier, and sub-agents get their own too (one level deep). In practice an "instance" is an install: the informational bootstrap draft gives each install one identity, so several processes under one install may share it. The resource sees the agent identifier only in agent-identity and resource-managed access; in the three person-based modes it is deliberately left out, for privacy and so resources cannot lock in a particular agent product.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: defined, but hidden from the resource in three of the five access modes.

claims.text: Visible only in two modes.
claims.quote: The agent identifier reaches a resource only in this mode and in resource-managed access.

claims.text: Not in the other three.
claims.quote: In the other three, no token the resource reads carries one

claims.quote: Each install's durable key is the basis for one agent identity.

claims.text: Sub-agents have their own identity.
claims.quote: A sub-agent has its own agent identity

claims.text: Only one level of sub-agents.
claims.quote: Delegation is at most one level deep

rows.short: Yes, if the agent has a person server
rows.answer: Partly. If the agent has a person server, the resource can require a person token, which tells it which person the agent acts for. The identifier is pseudonymous and different at each resource, so resources cannot correlate the person across services. Having a person server is optional: an agent without one can only use agent-identity or resource-managed access, where the resource runs its own sign-in if it needs to know the person.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: defined by the protocol, but only available when the agent has an (optional) person server.

claims.text: The resource learns the person from a person token.
claims.quote: The resource verifies the token, learns which person the agent acts for, and applies its own access control on that identity.

claims.text: The person server is optional.
claims.quote: An agent MAY have a person server, declared via the ps claim in the agent token.

claims.text: Without one, no person token.
claims.quote: An agent with no PS cannot obtain a person token, so agent-token and interaction are the whole of what is available to it.

claims.text: Pseudonymous per resource.
claims.quote: The PS SHOULD provide a pairwise pseudonymous user identifier (sub) per resource

rows.short: HTTP Message Signature plus key-bound token
rows.answer: An HTTP Message Signature (RFC 9421) on every request, covering the method, host, path and the Signature-Key header (plus a digest of the body for server endpoints). The request also carries a JWT: the agent token, a person token or an auth token, each containing the agent's public key. The verifier checks that this key signed the request, so every token is proof of possession and useless without the private key.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a signed credential on every request, with proof of possession (stronger than MCP Authorization's bearer token).

claims.text: Required signature coverage.
claims.quote: The signature MUST cover the following derived components and header fields:

claims.text: Tokens carry the agent's key.
claims.quote: Agents MUST use the jwt scheme, presenting a token that carries their public key in cnf

claims.text: Key must match the signature.
claims.quote: Verify cnf.jwk matches the key used to sign the HTTP request.

claims.text: Not bearer tokens.
claims.quote: It is not a bearer credential — cnf binds it to the agent's signing key

rows.answer: Very short for signatures, short for tokens. Servers reject a signature created more than 60 seconds ago by default. Person and auth tokens MUST NOT last more than 1 hour; agent tokens SHOULD NOT last more than 24 hours. There is no nonce, so the same signed request could be replayed within the 60-second window unless the server keeps an optional replay cache.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a specific short window that verifiers enforce (same as Visa TAP).

claims.text: 60-second signature window.
claims.quote: The default window is 60 seconds; servers MAY advertise a different window via metadata

claims.text: Person tokens up to 1 hour.
claims.quote: Person tokens MUST NOT have a lifetime exceeding 1 hour

claims.text: Auth tokens up to 1 hour.
claims.quote: Auth tokens MUST NOT have a lifetime exceeding 1 hour

claims.text: Agent tokens up to 24 hours (recommended).
claims.quote: Agent tokens SHOULD NOT have a lifetime exceeding 24 hours.

claims.text: No nonce.
claims.quote: This profile defines no nonce mechanism.

rows.answer: Yes. The server verifies the HTTP signature and its 60-second window, verifies the presented JWT with the issuer's keys (found through the issuer's well-known metadata), checks that the token has not expired, and checks that the key inside the token is the one that signed the request. No prior registration with the agent is needed.
rows.rating_reason: Green: verifiable against published keys with no prior relationship (same as MCP Authorization, Web Bot Auth and Visa TAP).

claims.quote: Verify exp is in the future, judged by the verifier's own clock.

claims.text: No registration needed.

rows.short: Yes, by the agent's own key
rows.answer: Yes for the agent. Every request is signed with a key that belongs to that specific agent instance, and the token presented binds that key, so the resource verifies the actual sender rather than a provider-wide key or a bearer token. The user is authenticated by the person server, not by the resource: a person token gives a stable pseudonym and makes no claim about how the person's identity was checked.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the resource verifies per-agent proof on every request, unlike the provider-level keys of Web Bot Auth and Visa TAP.

claims.quote: Every agent instance has its own identifier and signing key

claims.text: Same key in person tokens.
claims.quote: The person token's cnf.jwk is the same key that signed the request

claims.text: No identity proofing implied.

rows.answer: Yes. In the person-server modes the agent receives an auth token with scopes the resource defined and the person approved, and the granted scope can never be broader than what the resource offered. An optional account claim limits access to one account. In agent-identity mode there are no scopes; the resource simply decides based on who the agent is. Companion drafts add finer, operation-level authorization (R3) and spending ceilings per resource (Budgets).
rows.rating_reason: Green: scoped permissions in the normal person-server flow, enforced by the resource (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: No broader than offered.
claims.quote: MUST NOT be broader than the resource token's scope.

claims.text: Account binding.
claims.quote: Scope says what the agent may do; account says which account it may do it to.

claims.text: Identity-only mode has no scopes.
claims.quote: The resource verifies the agent's identity and applies its own access control, granting or denying based on who the agent is

claims.quote: enables structured, vocabulary-based authorization for resource access

claims.text: Budgets adds spending ceilings (companion draft).
claims.quote: A budget is a ceiling on what an agent may consume at one resource

rows.answer: Yes. The person server handles the person's consent before issuing tokens when needed, and the person can approve missions (task descriptions the agent proposes). An agent can also ask the person server for permission before local actions such as sending an email. The consent screen must separate what the resource says from what the agent claims. Approval can be delegated to a supervision server, which may be software rather than a person.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a defined approval step before access in the person-server flow (same as MCP Authorization); note that approval may be delegated to software.

rows.short: Agent provider and person server; resource decides
rows.answer: Partly. The agent provider vouches for its agents (it is trusted to issue agent tokens only to agents it authorizes), and the person server vouches for the person and their consent. But the resource decides for itself which agent providers and person servers to accept: it can trust an agent whose key it knows or whose domain it trusts, and in three-party mode any person server can assert to any resource. AAuth defines no registry or list of trusted providers.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: vouching parties are defined, but choosing which to trust is left to each resource, with no shared registry.

claims.text: The agent provider vouches for agents.
claims.quote: Trusted by the person to issue agent tokens only to authorized agents.

claims.text: Resources decide which agents to trust.
claims.quote: A resource MAY also authorize on the agent's identity alone, without any interaction, when the agent's key is already known or its domain is trusted.

claims.text: Any person server can assert.

claims.text: Searched for a registry, allowlist or trust framework for agent providers or person servers. None is defined.

rows.answer: Partly. Revocation is defined: servers SHOULD publish a revocation endpoint, and an agent provider revoking an agent token triggers a cascade through the person server to the person tokens and auth tokens issued to that agent, at agent level rather than provider level. Gaps: an agent token presented directly to a resource has no revocation path (up to 24 hours), and a server without a revocation endpoint keeps honouring tokens until they expire.

claims.quote: A resource that accepts an agent token directly has no revocation path

claims.text: No endpoint, no revocation.

rows.answer: No. Agent provider metadata includes a name, description, logo, documentation and terms or privacy links, but no contact or abuse channel. A person server may keep its own channel to the person (e.g. email or push notifications), but that is for approvals and alerts to the person, not a way for a service to reach whoever is responsible for an agent.

claims.quote: A PS MAY also maintain a direct channel to the person, such as email, push notification, or messaging, for out-of-band approvals, notifications, and revocation alerts.

rows.answer: No. The companion AAuth Events draft lets resources send events to an agent through its agent provider, which is a channel to the agent, not between services. Revocations travel between the parties involved in a grant, but there is no way for one service to warn others about a misbehaving agent.
rows.rating_reason: Red: not addressed (same as the calibration examples).

rows.answer: No. Nothing identifies the AI model. Agent tokens may carry extra claims, and the draft expects companion specifications to define some (e.g. software attestation or platform integrity), but none for the model exists yet. An optional platform parameter describes where the agent runs, for display at consent.
rows.rating_reason: Red: nothing identifies the model; an extension point exists but is not yet used for this.

goals_reading.access_control: Strong when a person server is used: the resource gets scoped, person-approved auth tokens bound to the agent's key. In agent-identity mode the resource decides on who the agent is, with no scopes.
goals_reading.incident_response: Access can be cut off per agent through the revocation cascade, and tokens expire within an hour. An agent token presented directly to a resource cannot be revoked and lasts up to 24 hours, and servers without a revocation endpoint keep honouring tokens until they expire.
goals_reading.accountability: Each agent is bound to exactly one person at the person server, which can keep a mission log and audit records. Resources see a per-resource pseudonym for the person, and the specific agent only in the two simplest modes.

summary: The Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP) lets an AI agent, such as ChatGPT, run a purchase against a merchant's own checkout on behalf of a buyer, while the merchant stays the seller of record and keeps payments on its own payment provider. It is aimed at three groups: merchants (called sellers), agent platforms, and payment service providers (PSPs). OpenAI and Stripe maintain it as founding maintainers, with Meta now also listed. It is published on GitHub under Apache 2.0 with dated releases, the latest being 2026-04-17, but the repository still labels the protocol as beta.

ACP is mainly a set of REST APIs that the merchant hosts: the agent creates, updates and completes checkout sessions, sending a bearer API key on every call and, as a recommendation, a signature over the JSON body with a timestamp. Payment details go to the merchant's PSP, which returns a one-time token limited by an allowance (maximum amount, currency, merchant, checkout session, expiry). The merchant can require extra buyer steps such as 3-D Secure, run through a delegated authentication API. ACP does not define how API keys are issued, who vouches for an agent platform, per-agent identity, revocation, contact channels or model identity; request signing is still informally specified.
how_it_works: Setup, outside the protocol: the merchant and the agent platform agree to work together and set up an API key (the specification does not say who issues it) and, if signatures are used, the accepted signature algorithms. The merchant may also publish a discovery document at /.well-known/acp.json.

The agent (e.g. ChatGPT) calls the merchant's POST /checkout_sessions with the items and, optionally, buyer and address details, sending Authorization: Bearer with the API key, an API-Version and an Idempotency-Key, and as a recommendation a Signature and Timestamp header.

The merchant checks the API key and, if used, the signature and timestamp, then returns the authoritative cart, its payment handlers and any required buyer interventions (e.g. 3-D Secure or biometric).

For card payments the agent sends the card details to the merchant's PSP (POST /agentic_commerce/delegate_payment), which returns a one-time vault token that can only be used within the allowance: maximum amount, currency, merchant, checkout session and expiry time.
If the merchant asks for 3-D Secure, the agent runs it through the delegated authentication API with the merchant's chosen authentication provider, and the buyer may be challenged by the card issuer.

The agent completes the session with the token (and any authentication result). The merchant charges the token through its PSP, creates the order, and sends order updates to the agent platform by signed webhook.

notes: Name collision: 'ACP' is also used for the Agent Communication Protocol (IBM BeeAI, later merged into A2A), the Agent Client Protocol (Zed, editor to coding agent) and AGNTCY's Agent Connect Protocol. This analysis covers the Agentic Commerce Protocol by OpenAI and Stripe.

Version: the latest dated release is 2026-04-17. The RFC design documents in rfcs/ are not snapshotted per release; their headers carry older version dates and statuses Draft or Proposal, and they were read at commit 7fdd78d. Where the RFCs and the released OpenAPI differ, both are cited.

Inconsistency: the delegate payment RFC says the client MUST sign requests (section 2.2) but lists the Signature header as RECOMMENDED (section 2.3); the checkout OpenAPI describes Signature as an HMAC for webhook verification, the delegate payment OpenAPI as a detached JSON signature.
Most RFC text uses RFC 2119 keywords. Where the requirement tag has an asterisk, the point rests on schema optionality or the lowercase word 'optional' rather than a keyword.

Stripe's documentation describes ACP's delegate authentication as delegating authorization with OAuth 2.0, while the specification at this commit defines delegate authentication as 3-D Secure 2 only and lists OAuth 2.0 identity linking as future work. This analysis follows the specification.

summary: The Agent Name Service (ANS) gives each AI agent a verifiable name tied to a domain name, so that one agent can check that another really belongs to the organisation it claims and is running the software version it registered. It answers questions like whether a supplier's invoicing agent is genuine or a look-alike. ANS grew out of an OWASP paper and IETF draft; GoDaddy built and runs a production registry, and the project is now a Linux Foundation series (LF Projects). The specifications in its GitHub repository are marked DRAFT and are newer than the companion IETF draft, an individual submission whose -01 revision dates from April 2026.

An agent operator registers an agent with a Registration Authority (RA), proving control of its domain. The RA issues certificates, including an Identity Certificate naming the agent and version (ans://v1.0.0.agent.example.com), publishes DNS records and seals every event into a public, append-only Transparency Log. When one agent calls another, the callee checks the caller's certificate (by mutual TLS or a per-request DPoP proof) plus a log receipt and a short-lived status token, so revoked agents are refused within about an hour. ANS deliberately covers authentication only: authorization, acting on behalf of users, trust scoring and contact details are left to the service or to other specifications.
how_it_works: The agent's operator registers the agent at a Registration Authority (RA): it proves control of the agent's domain (ACME DNS-01) and submits certificate requests, receiving a Server Certificate and, optionally, an Identity Certificate from the RA's private CA that names the agent and version.
The RA seals an AGENT_REGISTERED event into the Transparency Log (TL), and the operator publishes DNS records, including an _ans-badge record pointing to the agent's entry in the log.
In the background, the calling agent fetches its own log receipt (proof its registration is in the log) and a status token (proof it is currently active, valid for about an hour).

On each request, the caller proves possession of its Identity Certificate key: in the TLS handshake (Method A, mutual TLS) or with a signed DPoP proof bound to the method, URL and content (Method B), sending the receipt and status token in HTTP headers.

The callee (the receiving agent) verifies the certificate or proof, the receipt and status token against the TL's keys (or queries a trusted TL for the badge), checks that names and fingerprints match and that the agent is not revoked, then applies its own authorization policy.

rows.short: RA, TL, agent host provider, caller, callee, monitors
rows.answer: Registration Authority (RA): verifies domain control, issues certificates through its private CA and seals events, acting as a notary rather than a judge. Transparency Log (TL): append-only log that seals events and serves badges, receipts and status tokens. Agent Hosting Provider (AHP): the operator who registers and revokes agents and publishes DNS records. Caller and callee: the agent sending a request and the agent serving it. Integrity monitors (AIM): external services that report discrepancies. Verifiers and discovery services consume the outputs.

protocol.name: AP2
protocol.spec_version: AP2 v0.2 (git tag v0.2.0, commit b4587ac)
protocol.maintainer: Google (repository google-agentic-commerce/AP2); donated to the FIDO Alliance, where standardisation continues
protocol.newer_version_note: v0.2.0 is the latest release. The main branch is 4 commits ahead (changelog, contribution guide, README, lockfile only); the specification text is identical.

summary: The Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) gives merchants and payment providers cryptographic proof that a user really approved a purchase made by an AI shopping agent. Because an AI agent can be manipulated (e.g. by prompt injection), AP2 treats every agent as a potential attacker and asks for a signed, user-approved mandate before a checkout is completed or a payment credential is released. It sits on top of a commerce protocol such as Google's Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) or A2A. Google published AP2 in September 2025 and released v0.2 in April 2026, when it donated the protocol to the FIDO Alliance; the version number is pre-1.0 and standardisation continues there.

The shopping agent prepares a Checkout Mandate (what is bought, bound to a merchant-signed checkout) and a Payment Mandate (how it is paid). A Trusted Surface, a non-AI interface such as a wallet, shows them to the user and has them signed, either with the user's own digital credential or with the agent provider's key. If the user is present, they approve the exact checkout; if not, they approve limits (merchants, items, amounts, budget, dates) and the agent signs the final mandate with its own key. Merchants and payment providers verify signatures and limits and return signed receipts that serve as dispute evidence. AP2 leaves agent identification, revocation, contact and model identity to other layers.
how_it_works: Setup: the verifiers (merchant, credential provider, payment processor) decide whom they trust to vouch for user approval: issuers of user credentials (e.g. a wallet or bank) or a list of trusted agent providers.
The shopping agent builds a checkout with the merchant through a commerce protocol (e.g. UCP); the merchant returns a merchant-signed Checkout JWT.

The agent prepares Checkout and Payment Mandate content and sends it to a Trusted Surface, which shows it to the user and obtains consent. The result is a signed SD-JWT mandate: a closed mandate for the exact checkout (user present) or an open mandate with limits and the agent's public key (user not present).
In the autonomous case, the agent later signs a closed mandate for a specific checkout with its own key and presents it together with the open mandate, disclosing only the parts that are needed.

The credential provider verifies the Payment Mandate before releasing a payment credential; the merchant verifies the Checkout Mandate (signature chain, checkout hash, limits) before completing the checkout. Each verifier returns a signed receipt, and the mandates and receipts together form dispute evidence.

rows.answer: A protocol in which an AI shopping agent obtains user-approved, signed Checkout and Payment Mandates through a non-AI Trusted Surface, so that merchants and payment providers can verify what the user authorised before completing a purchase or releasing a payment credential.

protocol.spec_version: ERC-8004 (ERCS/erc-8004.md at commit 503591a, status Draft)
protocol.maintainer: ERC authors (M. De Rossi, MetaMask; D. Crapis, Ethereum Foundation; J. Ellis, Google; E. Reppel, Coinbase) through the Ethereum ERC process
protocol.newer_version_note: Commit 503591a is the last change to the file; it is unchanged at the ERCs repository head (7214b22, 2026-11-17). The ERC moved to Review in October 2025 and an editor returned it to Draft on 2026-01-13.

summary: ERC-8004, "Trustless Agents", is an Ethereum standard proposal for finding AI agents and judging whether to trust them when there is no existing relationship. It defines three public registries as smart contracts on a blockchain: an Identity Registry that gives each agent an on-chain identifier pointing to a registration file, a Reputation Registry where clients post feedback about agents, and a Validation Registry where independent validators record checks of an agent's work. Its authors come from MetaMask, the Ethereum Foundation, Google and Coinbase. It is a Draft ERC: it reached Review in October 2025 and was returned to Draft in January 2026. Its reference registries are deployed on Ethereum mainnet and several other chains.

An agent's owner registers it as an ERC-721 token (an NFT), whose URI points to a JSON file listing the agent's name and services, such as A2A, MCP, ENS names, DIDs, wallets or an email address, and the trust models it supports. Anyone except the owner can post signed-number feedback and tags, and validators (e.g. re-execution with stake, zero-knowledge proofs, trusted execution environments) can post scores. A service deciding whether to deal with an agent can read these public signals, filtered by reviewers it trusts. ERC-8004 does not authenticate requests, carry credentials, define permissions or revocation, or identify users or models; it is a discovery and reputation layer meant to be combined with protocols such as A2A or MCP.
how_it_works: The agent's owner calls register() on the chain's Identity Registry, receiving an agentId (an ERC-721 token) whose agentURI points to the agent's registration file, hosted on HTTPS, IPFS or fully on-chain.

The registration file lists the agent's services (e.g. its A2A agent card, MCP endpoint, ENS name, DID, email) and the trust models it supports; optionally the owner proves control of an endpoint domain by publishing a matching /.well-known/agent-registration.json.

A client or service discovers the agent (e.g. by crawling the registry) and interacts with it through the listed protocol, such as A2A or MCP; ERC-8004 does not define that interaction or how the agent proves its identity in it.

Afterwards, clients post feedback (a value plus optional tags and an off-chain file) to the Reputation Registry, and the agent's owner can ask a validator to check its work, which records a 0 to 100 score in the Validation Registry.
Before trusting the agent, a service reads summaries of feedback from reviewers it chooses and validation results from validators it trusts, and decides by its own policy.
