protocol.name: ID-JAG (Cross App Access)
protocol.spec_version: draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-06
protocol.maintainer: IETF OAuth working group (editors A. Parecki, Okta; K. McGuinness; B. Campbell, Ping Identity)
protocol.newer_version_note: -06 is the latest published draft. The editors' main branch has one editorial fix after -06 (commit e47d778, 2026-11-09), which was not analysed.

summary: The Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG), informally called Cross-App Access (XAA), lets an application, such as an AI agent, get an access token for another company's API on behalf of a signed-in user without sending the user through a separate OAuth consent screen. It relies on an identity provider (IdP), e.g. an enterprise single sign-on service, that both applications already trust, so the organisation that runs the IdP decides centrally which applications may reach which other applications for its users. It is an IETF OAuth working group draft (-06, October 2026), edited by authors from Okta and Ping Identity, and still expected to change. Okta implements it.

The application exchanges the user's sign-in assertion at the IdP for an ID-JAG: a short signed token naming the user, the application's client ID at the target, the target authorization server and the granted scopes or resources. The target's authorization server checks the signature, issuer, audience, client and expiry, applies its own policy and issues its own access token; the ID-JAG can optionally be bound to the client's key (DPoP or mutual TLS). The receiving service therefore learns the user and the client application, with scoped access approved by IdP policy. It does not learn the individual agent instance or model, the draft has no per-request user approval, and it defines no revocation, contact or signalling mechanism.
how_it_works: Setup: the organisation's IdP is trusted by both the client application (e.g. an AI agent) and the resource application's authorization server for single sign-on, and an administrator allows the client to access that resource application for its users with certain scopes.
The user signs in to the client through the IdP; the client receives an identity assertion (an OpenID Connect ID Token or SAML assertion) and optionally a refresh token.

The client sends a Token Exchange request to the IdP with that assertion, naming the target authorization server (audience) and the resource and scopes it wants. The IdP authenticates the client, applies administrator policy and returns a signed ID-JAG, optionally bound to the client's DPoP key or certificate.

The client presents the ID-JAG to the resource authorization server's token endpoint (JWT bearer grant), normally with client authentication. The server checks the type, trusted issuer, signature, audience, client_id, expiry, tenant and any key binding, then applies its own policy.

The resource authorization server issues its own access token, restricted to the granted resources and scopes. The client calls the API (resource server), which validates that token as usual. When the token expires, the client re-presents the ID-JAG or asks the IdP for a new one.

sources.title: Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-06 (Markdown source)

rows.short: IdP-brokered, scoped tokens for a user's apps
rows.answer: An IETF OAuth draft in which an application (e.g. an AI agent) exchanges a user's single sign-on assertion at a shared identity provider for a signed grant, which another application's authorization server checks and turns into its own scoped access token for that user, without a separate consent screen.

claims.text: The pattern is called Cross-App Access.
claims.quote: This pattern is informally referred to as Cross-App Access (XAA).

claims.text: A grant on behalf of a user without a direct user-approval step.
claims.quote: grants a client delegated access to a resource, typically in another trust domain, on behalf of a user without a direct user-approval step at the authorization server.

claims.text: The resource authorization server still issues its own access token.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server determines whether to honor a given ID-JAG, what scopes or authorization details to grant, and what access token to issue, applying its own local policy.

rows.answer: Access between applications that already share a single sign-on identity provider: enterprise SaaS integrations, customer-identity platforms calling developer SaaS components, email clients reaching calendars, and AI agents calling external tools. The ID-JAG travels in the body of an OAuth token request to the resource's authorization server, which verifies it; the API itself then only sees the access token that server issues.

claims.text: Applies beyond enterprise workforce IdPs.
claims.quote: Enterprise workforce identity providers are one common example, but the same trust pattern can also arise in customer identity, platform identity, and other federated application ecosystems.

claims.text: AI agents calling external tools is a named use case.
claims.section: Appendix: AI Agent using External Tools
claims.quote: AI agents are designed to perform complex tasks on behalf of users, often requiring integration with external tools provided by SaaS applications, internal services, or enterprise data sources.

claims.text: The ID-JAG is presented at the resource authorization server's token endpoint.
claims.quote: The Client makes an access token request to the Resource Authorization Server's token endpoint using the previously obtained Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant as a JWT Bearer Assertion

claims.text: The resource server only validates access tokens from its own authorization server.
claims.quote: Hosts protected resources and validates access tokens issued by the Resource Authorization Server.

rows.short: Client, IdP, resource AS, resource server
rows.answer: Client: the application that wants an access token to another application's API on behalf of a signed-in user. IdP Authorization Server (IdP): the OpenID Connect or SAML identity provider that issues sign-in assertions and ID-JAGs, and that the resource side already trusts. Resource Authorization Server (AS): checks ID-JAGs and issues access tokens. Resource Server (RS): hosts the API and validates those access tokens. The End-User is named in each ID-JAG, and an administrator grants clients permission in the IdP.

claims.text: Client role.
claims.quote: The application that wants to obtain an OAuth 2.0 access token on behalf of a signed-in user to an external/3rd party application's API (Resource Server below).

claims.text: IdP role.
claims.quote: In this specification, the IdP is the issuer that the Resource Authorization Server already trusts for SSO and subject resolution for the target user accounts.

claims.text: Resource Authorization Server role.
claims.quote: Issues OAuth 2.0 access tokens for protected resources provided by the Resource Server.

claims.text: Resource Server role.
claims.quote: Hosts protected resources and validates access tokens issued by the Resource Authorization Server.

claims.text: Administrator permission is a precondition.
claims.quote: Enterprise has granted the Client permission to act on behalf of users for the Resource Authorization Server with a set of scopes

rows.answer: Working-group draft. Version -06 was published on 31 October 2026 by the IETF OAuth working group, on the Standards Track, and is expected to change; it replaced the individual draft started in 2024. It depends on other drafts (Identity Chaining, the JWT DPoP grant). Okta documents its implementation as both identity provider and resource authorization server under the name Cross App Access.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: still a working-group draft, even though Okta has a named implementation (same as Web Bot Auth).

claims.text: Current revision is -06.
claims.quote: draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-06

claims.text: Depends on the Identity Chaining draft.
claims.quote: Identity Chaining intentionally leaves many details unspecified in order to support multiple use cases.

claims.text: Deployment: Okta issues ID-JAGs according to the connection an administrator allows.
claims.quote: The Okta authorization server issues the ID-JAG only for scoped access allowed in that connection.

rows.short: OAuth Token Exchange, JWT grants, DPoP, mTLS
rows.answer: A profile of the Identity Chaining draft, which combines OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) and JWT authorization grants (RFC 7523, RFC 7521). It uses JWT (RFC 7519) with explicit typing (RFC 8725), Resource Indicators (RFC 8707), Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396), Authorization Server and Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 8414, RFC 9728), and optional key binding with DPoP (RFC 9449) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705) via the cnf claim (RFC 7800). Sign-in uses OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0.

claims.text: Profiles Identity Chaining, Token Exchange and JWT grants.
claims.quote: XAA is built on top of OAuth 2.0 by profiling "Identity Chaining Across Trust Domains"

claims.text: Two sender-constraining mechanisms are defined.
claims.quote: This specification defines two sender-constraining mechanisms for the ID-JAG:

claims.text: Typed JWT.
claims.quote: Using typed JWTs is a recommendation of the JSON Web Token Best Current Practices as described in

rows.answer: Partly. Every ID-JAG must carry a client_id: the client identifier of the application at the resource authorization server, which the server checks against the client that authenticates. It names the client application (e.g. an AI agent product), not an individual agent; it may differ from the client ID used at the IdP, and can be an HTTPS URL when Client ID Metadata Documents are used. An optional act claim can name an actor, but the draft does not define how it is set.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: the identifier names the client application, shared by all its instances (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: client_id is a required claim naming the client at the resource authorization server.
claims.quote: REQUIRED - The client identifier of the OAuth 2.0 {{RFC6749}} client at the Resource Authorization Server that will act on behalf of the resource owner

claims.text: The server checks client_id against the authenticated client.
claims.quote: If the Client authenticates, the Resource Authorization Server MUST reject the request with an invalid_grant error unless the client_id claim identifies the authenticated client.

claims.text: Client ID Metadata Documents give a shared namespace of client IDs.
claims.quote: this acts as a shared global namespace of Client IDs

rows.short: No; actor handling out of scope
rows.answer: No. The ID-JAG identifies the user and the client application, not a specific running agent. A client may send an actor_token and the ID-JAG may carry an optional act claim naming an actor, but the draft states that processing the actor_token is out of scope and leaves the act claim to future profiles; it also warns that the client identity is not a substitute for actor identity.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no per-instance identifier is defined and actor processing is explicitly out of scope (same colour as all three calibration examples); the optional act claim was not counted because its content is undefined.

claims.text: Processing of an actor_token is out of scope.
claims.quote: If an actor_token is present, any processing of it is outside the scope of this specification.

claims.text: act is an optional claim.
claims.quote: When present, this claim identifies the actor that is acting on behalf of the subject

claims.text: Client identity does not stand in for actor identity.
claims.quote: The authenticated client identity is also not a substitute for actor identity.

rows.answer: Yes. Every ID-JAG must name the End-User in the sub claim, chosen by the IdP for this resource authorization server, with the IdP as issuer and a tenant claim for multi-tenant IdPs. The resource authorization server uses these, and optionally email, aud_sub or a SAML identifier, to find the matching local account (subject resolution). It can then carry the user into the access tokens it issues.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the principal is defined and sent to the receiving service as a requirement (stronger than all three calibration examples).

claims.text: sub is required and identifies the End-User.
claims.quote: The sub claim identifies the End-User in the subject namespace of the ID-JAG issuer.

claims.text: The same sub for a user at the same resource authorization server.
claims.quote: The IdP Authorization Server MUST include the same sub value for a given End-User in every ID-JAG it issues for the same Resource Authorization Server

claims.text: Tenant must be included for multi-tenant issuers.
claims.quote: When an IdP Authorization Server issues an ID-JAG, it MUST include the tenant claim if the issuer is multi-tenant.

claims.text: email or aud_sub are recommended for subject resolution.
claims.quote: It is RECOMMENDED that the ID-JAG contain an email {{OpenID.Core}} and/or aud_sub {{OpenID.Enterprise}} claim.

rows.answer: A signed JWT (the ID-JAG, typed oauth-id-jag+jwt) presented at the resource authorization server's token endpoint, normally together with OAuth client authentication; the API then receives that server's own access token on each request. By default the ID-JAG and the access token are bearer credentials, usable by whoever holds them. Optionally the IdP binds the ID-JAG to the client's DPoP key or mTLS certificate (cnf claim), and the server must then check proof of possession and may bind the access token to the same key.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a defined, verifiable credential is required to obtain access, and each API request carries the resource server's own token (same as MCP Authorization); proof of possession is optional.

claims.text: The ID-JAG is a typed JWT.
claims.quote: The typ of the JWT indicated in the JWT header MUST be oauth-id-jag+jwt.

claims.text: Client authentication or a sender-constrained ID-JAG is required.
claims.quote: It MUST reject a request that has neither client authentication nor a sender-constrained ID-JAG

claims.text: Proof of possession is required when the ID-JAG has a cnf claim.
claims.quote: When an ID-JAG contains a cnf claim, proof of possession of the corresponding private key or X.509 certificate MUST be demonstrated when using the ID-JAG at the Resource Authorization Server.

claims.text: Without a DPoP proof, no binding is added.
claims.section: DPoP Key Binding During Token Exchange
claims.quote: If no DPoP proof is presented, the IdP issues an ID-JAG without a cnf claim.

claims.text: Without key binding, anyone with a copy can present it.
claims.quote: Without the key binding, anyone holding a copy of the ID-JAG could present it.

rows.answer: Partly. Every ID-JAG must carry an expiry time (exp), and the resource authorization server must reject expired ones, but the draft sets no maximum; the examples use five minutes. The server may refuse ID-JAGs whose expiry is longer than its own policy, or accept each only once. The client may re-present an unexpired ID-JAG to get fresh access tokens, so its lifetime also limits how long access can be renewed without the IdP.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: expiry is required but no specific limit is given; the verifier may apply its own maximum (MCP Authorization and Web Bot Auth are yellow for the same reason; Visa TAP's eight-minute rule is green).

claims.text: exp is required.
claims.quote: REQUIRED - as defined in {{Section 4.1.4 of RFC7519}}.

claims.text: The server can reject long expiries or accept each ID-JAG once.
claims.quote: the Resource Authorization Server can reject an ID-JAG with an exp longer than its policy allows, or accept each ID-JAG only once by tracking its jti

claims.text: The ID-JAG can be re-submitted to get new access tokens.
claims.quote: When the access token has expired, clients MAY re-submit the original Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant to obtain a new Access Token.

claims.text: expires_in is only recommended in the response; the example shows 300 seconds.
claims.quote: RECOMMENDED - The lifetime in seconds of the authorization grant.

rows.short: Yes, against the trusted IdP's keys
rows.answer: Yes. The resource authorization server checks the JWT type, that the issuer is an IdP it trusts, the signature using keys from that issuer's published metadata, that the audience is exactly itself, the client_id, the expiry and other JWT grant rules, the tenant, and any key binding. It needs a prior trust relationship with the IdP but none with the individual client beyond its normal OAuth registration.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the service validates the credential against published keys of its trusted issuer, with expiry checks (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.text: Issuer trust and signature checks.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server MUST reject the ID-JAG with an invalid_grant error if the iss claim does not identify an IdP Authorization Server it trusts.

claims.text: Keys come from the issuer's metadata.
claims.quote: It SHOULD obtain that issuer's keys from the jwks_uri in the issuer's metadata

claims.text: Audience check.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server MUST validate the aud (audience) claim of the ID-JAG.

claims.text: Validation covers issuer, signature, audience, expiry and client binding.
claims.quote: The ID-JAG MUST first be validated using the iss claim, signature, audience, expiration, and client binding according to this specification.

rows.property: Authentication of the agent or user
rows.short: Client app auth; user signs in at IdP
rows.answer: No, not of the individual agent or the user. The resource authorization server should authenticate the client application with its OAuth client credentials (or rely on a key-bound ID-JAG instead), which proves the application, not one agent instance. The user signs in at the IdP, and the server relies on the IdP's assertion in the ID-JAG, optionally with the time and methods of that sign-in (auth_time, amr, acr).
rows.rating_reason: Red: the service checks an application-level client credential and a grant issued by the IdP, which signs the user in (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Client authentication is recommended at the resource authorization server.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server SHOULD require client authentication.

claims.text: Without client authentication, the server relies on the IdP.
claims.quote: It then relies on the IdP Authorization Server

claims.text: User authentication is delegated to the IdP.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server not only delegates user authentication to that IdP, but also relies on the IdP-issued grant as input to delegated authorization

rows.answer: Yes. The IdP grants scopes, resource identifiers and optionally structured authorization details (Rich Authorization Requests), based on administrator policy, and writes them into the ID-JAG. The resource authorization server must process them, may narrow them by its own policy, and must restrict the access token to the granted resources. The meaning of each scope is defined by the resource side.
rows.rating_reason: Green: scoped permissions are part of the normal flow and enforced by the service (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: The IdP evaluates policy for the requested access.
claims.quote: The IdP Authorization Server evaluates administrator-defined policy for the token exchange request and determines if the client should be granted access to act on behalf of the subject for the target audience, resources, scopes, and authorization details.

claims.text: The access token is restricted to the granted resources.
claims.quote: The access token MUST be restricted to resources in the resource claim

claims.text: The server may grant a subset of scopes.
claims.quote: The granted scopes MAY be a subset of the scopes in the ID-JAG issued by the IdP Authorization Server.

claims.text: Structured authorization details are supported.
claims.quote: This claim enables Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) support, allowing structured authorization requests beyond simple scope strings.

rows.short: No; replaced by IdP admin policy
rows.answer: No, by design. The ID-JAG replaces the user's consent at the resource authorization server with a decision by the IdP based on administrator policy; the resource side does not ask the user again. The user only signs in to the client through the IdP, which may require step-up sign-in. Clients that cannot authenticate to the IdP should fall back to the normal OAuth flow with interactive consent.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no user approval step for the access; approval is an administrator policy at the IdP, outside the request flow (MCP Authorization is green because its flow includes user consent).

claims.text: No user consent at the token exchange step.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server does not need to obtain user consent directly from the resource owner again at the token exchange step.

claims.text: The grant works without a direct user-approval step.
claims.quote: on behalf of a user without a direct user-approval step at the authorization server.

claims.text: Fallback to interactive consent for clients that cannot authenticate to the IdP.
claims.quote: where the user can interactively consent to the access delegation.

rows.short: The IdP the service already trusts for SSO
rows.answer: The identity provider that the resource application already trusts for single sign-on. The resource authorization server must reject ID-JAGs from issuers it does not trust and must be configured for each trusted IdP. The IdP issues an ID-JAG only when its administrator policy allows that client to act for that user at that target, so a valid ID-JAG means the organisation's IdP vouched for this client and user.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the protocol names a party that vouches (the trusted IdP), and only grants it approved are accepted (same as MCP Authorization and Visa TAP).

claims.text: Only trusted issuers are accepted.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server MUST reject the ID-JAG with an invalid_grant error if the iss claim does not identify an IdP Authorization Server it trusts.

claims.text: Each trusted issuer must be configured.
claims.quote: for each trusted issuer the Resource Authorization Server MUST be configured to recognize that issuer

claims.text: The IdP decides by administrator policy.
claims.quote: The IdP Authorization Server evaluates administrator-defined policy for the token exchange request and determines if the client should be granted access to act on behalf of the subject for the target audience, resources, scopes, and authorization details.

rows.short: Not defined; IdP can stop new grants
rows.answer: Not defined by the draft. Its design gives the IdP a central cut-off: the resource side should not issue refresh tokens, so renewed access needs a fresh or re-presented ID-JAG, and the IdP should be able to revoke refresh tokens and end a user's sessions. But an ID-JAG already issued stays usable until it expires, and access tokens already issued last as long as the resource server set (the examples use 24 hours). Granularity is per user or client, not per agent instance.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no revocation mechanism reaching the service is defined; the SHOULD-level recommendations only limit renewal at the IdP, so coverage is none (same colour as the calibration examples, which also leave revocation to other parties).

claims.text: No refresh token from the resource authorization server.
claims.quote: The Resource Authorization Server SHOULD NOT return a Refresh Token when an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant is exchanged for an Access Token

claims.text: The IdP should be able to revoke refresh tokens and sessions.
claims.quote: IdP Authorization Servers SHOULD also provide a mechanism to revoke Refresh Tokens and to invalidate outstanding sessions for a subject

claims.text: The ID-JAG can be re-submitted until it expires.
claims.quote: When the access token has expired, clients MAY re-submit the original Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant to obtain a new Access Token.

rows.answer: No. The draft defines no contact or escalation channel for the client's operator or the user. In practice the resource side has a configured trust relationship with the IdP and an OAuth registration for the client, which give it known parties to contact, but that is outside the protocol.

rows.answer: No. The draft asks the IdP to record each token exchange so it can spot unusual patterns, such as a client requesting grants for unfamiliar targets, but this is local logging. It defines no way for a resource application to warn the IdP or other services about a misbehaving client.
rows.rating_reason: Red: not addressed (same as all three calibration examples).

rows.answer: No. The ID-JAG names the user, the client application and optionally an actor, but nothing about which AI model is behind an agent. The AI agent use case treats the agent as an ordinary OAuth client.

goals_reading.access_control: The resource application receives an IdP-approved grant naming the user and the client application, limited by scopes, resources and optional structured details, and can narrow it further by its own policy.
goals_reading.incident_response: The organisation's IdP can stop issuing new grants for a user or client, but grants and access tokens already issued keep working until they expire; no revocation reaches the resource side, and there is no way to stop one agent instance.
goals_reading.accountability: Each access can be traced to the user (sub, tenant), the client application (client_id) and the IdP that issued the grant; not to an individual agent instance or model.

notes: The receiving service is taken to be the resource application: its authorization server receives and checks the ID-JAG, and its resource server (API) receives the access tokens that server issues.
The Markdown source has no section numbers, so claims cite section headings; where a heading appears twice (e.g. Processing Rules), the parent section is given in brackets.
"Cross App Access" is also Okta's product name, and MCP has an enterprise-managed authorization extension built on ID-JAG. This analysis covers only the IETF draft.
The IETF archive copy and the Okta page could not be downloaded by the quote checker; their quotes were checked with a web tool.
open_questions: The draft sets no maximum lifetime for an ID-JAG, and a client may re-present an unexpired one to get new access tokens. How long will deployments let ID-JAGs live, given that this lifetime also limits how fast an IdP-side cut-off takes effect?
Future profiles may define actor_token processing and the act claim. Would that give resource applications a per-agent or per-instance identifier?
The step-up section still contains a TBD note about requesting the ID-JAG during the authorization request; this may change in later drafts.

protocol.name: AI Agent Authentication and Authorization (draft-klrc-aiagent-auth)
protocol.full_name: AI Agent Authentication and Authorization, draft-klrc-aiagent-auth
protocol.spec_version: draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03
protocol.maintainer: P. Kasselman (Defakto Security), J. Lombardo (AWS), Y. Rosomakho (Zscaler), B. Campbell (Ping Identity), N. Steele (OpenAI), A. Parecki (Okta); individual Internet-Draft, later adopted by the IETF WIMSE working group
protocol.newer_version_note: -03 is the last revision under this name. The IETF datatracker lists it as replaced by the WIMSE working-group draft draft-ietf-wimse-aims (-00 September 2026, -01 2 November 2026), developed in the same repository. The successor was not analysed.

summary: Many groups are inventing new identity and authorization protocols for AI agents. This Informational Internet-Draft argues that existing standards already cover most needs and shows how to combine them. It treats an agent as a workload, like any other running service, and gives best practices for identifying, authenticating, authorizing and monitoring it. It is written by authors from Defakto, AWS, Zscaler, Ping Identity, OpenAI and Okta. Version -03 (July 2026) is the last version under this name: the IETF WIMSE working group has since adopted it as draft-ietf-wimse-aims, which is not analysed here. No deployment of the framework itself is named.

Each agent must have exactly one workload identifier (WIMSE, possibly a SPIFFE ID) and short-lived credentials bound to a key, issued after an assessment of its environment. Services authenticate the agent with mutual TLS, WIMSE proof tokens or HTTP Message Signatures, and grant access through OAuth access tokens. The token names the agent (client_id) and the user it acts for (sub), with user approval and CIBA step-up for sensitive actions. Revocation and monitoring rely on OpenID Shared Signals, and audit logs are mandatory. It defines no new messages, no model identity, no contact channel, and no identifier for individual running copies.
how_it_works: When an agent is deployed, its platform's provisioning system (e.g. SPIFFE) checks the agent's environment and issues it a short-lived credential bound to its unique WIMSE identifier (e.g. an X.509 certificate or a Workload Identity Token), and rotates it automatically. The language model never sees these credentials.

To act for a user, the agent sends the user to the authorization server, where the user signs in (preferably with a passkey) and approves the access. The agent then authenticates with its own credential (not a static secret) to redeem an access token naming the user in sub and the agent in client_id. Acting for itself, it uses client credentials or a JWT grant.
The agent calls a tool, service or LLM, authenticating with mutual TLS, a WIMSE proof token or an HTTP Message Signature using its key, and presents the access token.

The service checks the agent's proof, validates the access token (directly or by introspection) and decides on the request using the agent and user identifiers, scopes and its own policy. For sensitive actions the authorization server can require extra user approval, e.g. through CIBA.

Inside the service, the access token is swapped for a Transaction Token; to reach another domain, the agent uses Identity and Authorization Chaining to get a token from that domain's authorization server.

Participants may subscribe to Shared Signals (CAEP or RISC) events and must stop using revoked access promptly. All parties keep tamper-evident audit logs of the agent, the user, the action and the decision.

rows.short: Best-practice framework composing WIMSE, SPIFFE, OAuth, SSF
rows.answer: An Informational IETF draft that treats AI agents as workloads and tells deployers to give each agent a WIMSE or SPIFFE identity with short-lived key-bound credentials, authenticate it with mutual TLS or signed proofs, authorize it with OAuth access tokens naming the agent and the user, and monitor and revoke through Shared Signals.

claims.text: The document proposes best practices built on existing standards.
claims.quote: This document proposes best practices for authentication and authorization of AI agent interactions.

claims.text: It defines no new protocols.
claims.quote: Rather than defining new protocols, this document describes how existing and widely deployed standards can be applied or extended to establish agent authentication and authorization.

rows.short: Agents calling LLMs, tools, services, other agents
rows.answer: Any agent calling a large language model, tools, services, resources or other agents, whether for a user, for a system or on its own behalf, inside one organisation or across domains. Identity travels at the transport layer (mutual TLS) or in HTTP headers (proof tokens, HTTP Message Signatures), plus an OAuth access token; the receiving service verifies these itself, or a service mesh does. Communication inside or between tools and services is out of scope.

claims.text: Agents interact with LLMs and tools, services and resources.
claims.quote: An Agent is a workload that iteratively interacts with a Large Language Model (LLM) and a set of Tools, Services and Resources.

claims.text: Communication between tools is out of scope.
claims.quote: Communication within or between Tools, Services, and Resources is out of scope.

claims.text: Authentication can happen at either layer.
claims.quote: authentication can occur at either the transport layer or the application layer, and many deployments rely on a combination of both.

claims.text: mTLS is common in service meshes.
claims.quote: One example of this is the use of mTLS in service mesh architectures such as Istio or LinkerD.

rows.short: User/System, Agent, LLM, Tools, AS, AIMS
rows.answer: User or System: gives the agent a request or mission (a system can be a batch job or another agent). AI Agent: a workload that loops between the LLM and tools until its task ends. Large Language Model: chooses which tools to call. Tools, Services and Resources: the endpoints the agent calls, which can themselves be agents. OAuth authorization server: issues access tokens. Agent Identity Management System (AIMS): a conceptual set of functions (identity providers, provisioning, policy engines, enforcement points), not one product.

claims.text: The figure names User or System, Agent, LLM, and Tools, Services and Resources.
claims.quote: illustrates the high-level interaction model between the User or System, the AI Agent, the Large Language Model (LLM), Tools, Services, and Resources.

claims.text: A tool can itself be an agent.
claims.quote: A Tool endpoint may itself be implemented by another AI agent.

claims.text: AIMS is a conceptual model across components.
claims.quote: AIMS may be implemented by one component or distributed across multiple systems (such as identity providers, provisioning services, authorization servers, policy engines, and runtime enforcement points).

claims.text: The authorization server issues tokens.
claims.section: 10.2. Leverage OAuth 2.0 as a Delegation Authorization Framework
claims.quote: an Agent acts as an OAuth 2.0 Client to an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server

rows.short: Individual draft -03, replaced by WIMSE WG draft
rows.answer: Early proposal, since replaced. Version -03 (6 July 2026) is an individual Informational Internet-Draft; the WIMSE working group has adopted the work as draft-ietf-wimse-aims, now the active document. Several building blocks (WIMSE identifier, credentials and proof tokens, Transaction Tokens, Identity Chaining) are themselves still drafts, while SPIFFE and the OAuth RFCs are deployed. No deployment of the framework as such is named.
rows.rating_reason: Red: an individual draft with no named deployments of the framework; its working-group successor was not rated.

claims.text: At -03 the repository describes an individual draft.
claims.quote: This is the working area for the individual Internet-Draft, "Agent-to-Agent Authentication and Authorization".

claims.text: The repository now hosts the WIMSE working-group successor.
claims.quote: This is the working area for the IETF WIMSE Working Group Internet-Draft, "AI Identity Management System".

claims.text: Several building blocks are drafts.
claims.quote: The Workload Identity in Multi-System Environments (WIMSE) identifier as defined by {{!WIMSE-ID=I-D.ietf-wimse-identifier}} is the primary identifier for agents in this framework.

claims.text: Searched all sections for implementations or deployments of the framework; none named. No implementation of the framework is named.
claims.section: Searched all sections for implementations or deployments of the framework; none named

rows.short: WIMSE, SPIFFE, OAuth family, Txn-Tokens, SSF
rows.answer: Identity and credentials: WIMSE identifiers and workload credentials (drafts) and SPIFFE IDs and SVIDs. Authentication: mutual TLS, WIMSE Workload Proof Tokens (draft) and WIMSE HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). Authorization: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) with JWT access tokens (RFC 9068), introspection (RFC 7662), JWT and mTLS client authentication (RFC 7523, RFC 8705), Token Exchange (RFC 8693), the OAuth Security BCP (RFC 9700), Transaction Tokens and Identity Chaining (drafts), discovery (RFC 8414, RFC 9728) and CIBA. Monitoring: OpenID Shared Signals with CAEP and RISC.

claims.text: Built on SPIFFE, WIMSE, OAuth and SSF.
claims.quote: This document describes how AI Agents should leverage existing standards defined by SPIFFE {{SPIFFE}}, WIMSE, OAuth and OpenID SSF {{SSF}}.

claims.text: WIMSE defines WPTs and HTTP signatures for agents.
claims.quote: The WIMSE working group defines WIMSE Proof Tokens and HTTP Message Signatures as authentication mechanisms that may be used by agents.

claims.text: OAuth Security BCP applies.
claims.quote: The Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security as described in {{!OAUTH-BCP=RFC9700}} are applicable when requesting and using access tokens.

rows.short: One WIMSE/SPIFFE workload ID per agent
rows.answer: Yes, per agent, but not necessarily per running copy. Every agent must have exactly one WIMSE identifier, a URI that uniquely names a workload within a trust domain; it may be a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://trust-domain/path). In access tokens the agent appears as the OAuth client_id. The draft does not say whether separate running copies of the same agent get separate identifiers; in common SPIFFE deployments replicas of one service share an ID.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: each agent has a required identifier of its own, but the draft does not require each running copy to have one, so by the tie rule it is rated with identifiers that name the application (MCP Authorization) rather than green.

claims.text: Agents must be uniquely identified.
claims.quote: Agents MUST be uniquely identified in order to support authentication, authorization, auditing, and delegation.

claims.text: Exactly one WIMSE identifier per agent.
claims.quote: An agent participating in this framework MUST be assigned exactly one WIMSE identifier, which MAY be a SPIFFE ID.

claims.text: What a WIMSE identifier is.
claims.quote: A WIMSE identifier is a URI that uniquely identifies a workload within a trust domain.

claims.text: In access tokens the agent is client_id.
claims.quote: The access token includes the Agent identity as the 'client_id' claim as defined in {{Section 2.2 of OAUTH-ACCESSTOKEN-JWT}}.

claims.text: Searched 5 Agent Identity Management System, 6 Agent Identifier, 8 Agent Credential Provisioning for instance, replica or session. The draft does not address separate identifiers for running copies of one agent.
claims.section: Searched 5 Agent Identity Management System, 6 Agent Identifier, 8 Agent Credential Provisioning for instance, replica or session

rows.answer: Not defined. The draft identifies agents as workloads but never distinguishes one running copy, session or task of an agent from another, and defines no instance or session identifier. A deployment could give each running copy its own WIMSE identifier and credential, which the draft allows but does not require. Audit records must include a transaction or request correlation identifier, which identifies a request, not an agent instance.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no per-instance identifier is defined (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Searched all sections for instance, replica, session and sub-agent identifiers. No instance identifier.
claims.section: Searched all sections for instance, replica, session and sub-agent identifiers

claims.text: Audit records carry a request correlation identifier.
claims.quote: timestamp and transaction or request correlation identifier

rows.short: Yes, user or system in sub
rows.answer: Yes. When the agent acts for a user or a system, the access token carries that party's identifier in the sub claim (as in JWT access tokens, RFC 9068), and resource servers must use these identifiers, with the other claims, to decide on access. For opaque tokens the same information comes through introspection. When the agent acts on its own behalf, there is no separate principal.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the framework puts the delegating user or system in the access token the service receives, as part of its normal flow; MCP Authorization is red because it defines no such rule.

claims.text: The user or system is conveyed in sub.
claims.quote: When the Agent is acting on-behalf of another User or System, the User or System identifier is conveyed in the 'sub' claim as defined in {{Section 2.2 of OAUTH-ACCESSTOKEN-JWT}}.

claims.text: Resource servers must use these identifiers.
claims.quote: These identifiers MUST be used by resource servers protected by the OAuth 2.0 authorization service, along with other claims in the access token, to determine if access to a resource should be allowed.

claims.text: Opaque tokens give the same through introspection.
claims.quote: The introspection response provides the active state of the token and associated authorization attributes equivalent to those conveyed in structured tokens.

rows.short: Key-bound workload credential plus access token
rows.answer: A workload credential bound to the agent's key, plus an OAuth access token. The agent proves its identity with mutual TLS (X.509 certificate), a WIMSE Workload Proof Token (a signed JWT tied to the request, covering e.g. audience, expiry and a hash of the agent's token) or an HTTP Message Signature covering e.g. method, path and body digest; these are proof of possession. JWT-SVIDs and the access token are bearer tokens; -03 does not require sender-constrained access tokens. Static API keys are called an antipattern.
rows.rating_reason: Green: cryptographically bound credentials are required and presented in the normal flow; the answer notes which options are bearer (as for MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Credentials must be cryptographically bound.
claims.quote: Agents MUST possess credentials that provide a cryptographic binding to the agent identifier.

claims.text: WPTs give proof of possession tied to a message.
claims.quote: A WPT is defined as a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that binds an agent’s authentication to a specific message context, for example, an HTTP request, thereby providing proof of possession rather than relying on bearer semantics.

claims.text: WPT claims include audience, expiry, unique ID and a hash of the WIT.
claims.quote: They carry claims such as audience (aud), expiration (exp), a unique token identifier (jti), and a hash of the associated WIT (wth).

claims.text: HTTP Message Signatures cover request components.
claims.quote: The profile mandates signing of some request components (e.g., method, request-target, content digest, and the WIT itself) and supports optional response signing.

claims.text: JWT-SVIDs are bearer credentials.
claims.quote: JWT-SVIDs are short-lived bearer credentials used for JWT-based authentication.

claims.text: Static API keys are an antipattern.
claims.quote: Static API keys are an antipattern for agent identity.

claims.text: Searched 10.3 Use of OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens and 10.4 for DPoP, sender-constrained or certificate-bound access tokens. No sender-constraint requirement for access tokens.
claims.section: Searched 10.3 Use of OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens and 10.4 for DPoP, sender-constrained or certificate-bound access tokens

rows.answer: Short, but no number. Agent credentials SHOULD be short-lived and MUST carry an explicit expiry after which they are not accepted; the draft presents short lifetimes with automatic rotation as an alternative to explicit revocation. Proof tokens are typically short-lived. No maximum is given for workload credentials or access tokens, and verifiers are not told to reject long-lived ones.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: short lifetimes are recommended with no specific limit (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Short-lived recommended, expiry mandatory.
claims.quote: Agent credentials SHOULD be short-lived to minimize the risk of credential theft, MUST include an explicit expiration time after which it is no longer accepted

claims.text: Short lifetimes as an alternative to revocation.
claims.quote: It provides an alternative to explicit revocation mechanisms and simplifies lifecycle management in large, automated environments

claims.text: WPTs are typically short-lived.
claims.quote: WPTs are designed to work alongside WITs {{WIMSE-CRED}} and are typically short-lived to reduce the window for replay attacks.

rows.short: Yes, key proof and token validation
rows.answer: Yes. The receiving service verifies the agent's identity, possession of its key and the binding to the message (through the TLS handshake, the proof token or the HTTP signature), and checks that credentials have not expired. It validates JWT access tokens itself or asks its authorization server through introspection. Checking the workload credential needs the agent's trust-domain keys (e.g. a SPIFFE trust bundle), which in practice means prior setup between domains; the draft does not describe that distribution.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the service can validate both credentials with expiry checks, the access token through its own authorization server (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Receivers verify identity, key possession and message binding.
claims.quote: This design enables receiving systems to verify identity, key possession, and message binding at the application layer

claims.text: Access tokens are validated directly or by introspection.
claims.quote: JWT access tokens can be validated directly by resource servers while other formats that are opaque to the resource server can be validated through a mechanism that calls back to the authorization server

claims.text: Expired credentials are not accepted.
claims.quote: MUST include an explicit expiration time after which it is no longer accepted

claims.text: Searched 7 Agent Credentials, 9 Agent Authentication for trust bundle, key distribution and federation between trust domains. Trust-bundle distribution is not described.
claims.section: Searched 7 Agent Credentials, 9 Agent Authentication for trust bundle, key distribution and federation between trust domains

rows.property: Authentication of the agent or user
rows.short: Yes, agent's own key, per request
rows.answer: Yes, for the agent. The service authenticates the agent directly with the agent's own key: in the mutual TLS handshake, or per request through a WIMSE proof token or HTTP Message Signature, each tied to the agent's workload credential. SPIFFE-style provisioning gives each credential its own short-lived key. The user is authenticated by the authorization server (preferably with a passkey), not by the service. Which mechanism a deployment uses is its choice; the draft describes options rather than mandating one.
rows.rating_reason: Green: in the framework's normal flow the service verifies proof from the agent's own key; the calibration examples are red because they check only a token or a provider key.

claims.text: mTLS proves control of the agent's private key.
claims.quote: mTLS provides strong channel binding and cryptographic proof of control over the agent’s private key.

claims.text: WPTs are generated by the agent with its key.
claims.quote: WPTs are generated by the agent, using the private key matching the public key in the WIT.

claims.text: Services and others authenticate the agent.
claims.quote: the AI agent is a workload that needs an identifier and credentials so it can be authenticated by the Tools, Services, Resources, Large Language Model, System and the User

claims.text: Keys are ephemeral per credential with SPIFFE.
claims.quote: {{SPIFFE}} also provisions ephemeral cryptographic key material bound to each credential

claims.text: The user authenticates at the authorization server.
claims.quote: the user authenticates to the authorization server and explicitly approves the requested access.

rows.short: Yes, OAuth scopes and token claims
rows.answer: Yes. Access is granted through OAuth access tokens carrying claims such as scope, audience, client_id and sub, and resource servers decide using these together with their own policy, attribute or role systems. Agents SHOULD request only the minimum scopes needed, and Transaction Tokens narrow access inside a service to one transaction. How an agent turns its natural-language mission into specific permissions is out of scope.
rows.rating_reason: Green: scoped permissions in the access token are part of the normal flow and enforced by the service (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Access tokens carry scope and other claims.
claims.quote: which include claims such as 'client_id', 'sub', 'aud', 'scope', and other attributes relevant to authorization.

claims.text: Least privilege is recommended.
claims.quote: Agents SHOULD request only the minimum scopes and authorization details necessary to complete a task.

claims.text: Mission translation is out of scope.
claims.quote: The process through which the mission is translated into authorization requriements is out of scope of this specification.

claims.text: Transaction Tokens narrow access internally.
claims.quote: This results in a downscoped token that is bound to a specific transaction and cannot be used as an access token, with another transaction, or within the same transaction with modified transaction details

rows.answer: Yes, when the agent acts for a user. The user signs in at the authorization server and explicitly approves the access before a token is issued. For risky requests the authorization server SHOULD decline or obtain more approval, e.g. through CIBA (a push to the user's phone). Confirmation inside the agent's own interface does not count: it must be tied to a grant from the authorization server. Agents acting on their own behalf need no person, and the draft notes CIBA fits mid-task approval poorly.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a user approval step is part of the defined delegation flow, with step-up for sensitive actions (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: The user explicitly approves.
claims.quote: the user authenticates to the authorization server and explicitly approves the requested access.

claims.text: The authorization server can require more approval.
claims.quote: In such cases the authorization server SHOULD either decline the request or obtain additional authorization from the User.

claims.text: Local UI confirmation is not enough.
claims.quote: the agent MUST NOT treat local UI confirmation alone as sufficient authorization.

claims.text: CIBA has limits mid-execution.
claims.quote: CIBA itself only accounts for client initiation, which doesn't map well to cases that envision the need for User confirmation to occur mid-execution.

rows.answer: Two parties. The provisioning system (e.g. SPIFFE) vouches for the agent's identity: it checks signals about the agent and its environment (posture) and only then issues short-lived credentials. The authorization server vouches for access: it evaluates policy and issues the tokens the service accepts. The draft requires no particular posture mechanism or evidence, so how much the identity is worth depends on the deployment.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the framework names the parties that vouch (credential provisioner and authorization server), as MCP Authorization names its authorization server.

claims.text: Provisioning issues credentials after verification.
claims.quote: a provisioning component gathers workload and execution context signals, verifies them according to local policy, and, if verification succeeds, issues short-lived credentials for subsequent authentication and authorization.

claims.text: The authorization server evaluates policy and issues tokens.
claims.section: 10.2. Leverage OAuth 2.0 as a Delegation Authorization Framework
claims.quote: which receives the request, evaluate the authorization policy and returns an access token

claims.text: No posture mechanism is required.
claims.quote: This document does not require any particular posture assessment mechanism, evidence format, or verifier architecture.

rows.short: Optional via Shared Signals; short lifetimes
rows.answer: Partly. The main tool is short credential lifetimes, which the draft calls an alternative to explicit revocation. In addition, any participant MAY subscribe to OpenID Shared Signals events (CAEP or RISC, e.g. session revoked or subject disabled), and recipients must then stop using revoked authorization without undue delay. Subscription is optional and who sends which events is left open. Granularity depends on the event (a session, a user or the agent's identity).
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: revocation via signals is defined and enforced promptly once received, but subscribing is optional, so it may not reach every verifier; the calibration examples are red because they define none.

claims.text: Subscribing to signals is optional.
claims.quote: Any participant in the system, including the Agent, Tool, System, LLM or other resources and service MAY subscribe to change notifications using eventing mechanisms such as the OpenID Shared Signals Framework {{SSF}}

claims.text: Recipients must enforce revocation promptly.
claims.quote: Recipients of such signals MUST ensure that revoked or downgraded authorization is enforced without undue delay.

claims.text: Short lifetimes replace explicit revocation.
claims.quote: It provides an alternative to explicit revocation mechanisms and simplifies lifecycle management in large, automated environments

rows.answer: No. The draft defines no way for a service to reach whoever runs the agent. It requires tamper-evident audit logs, recommends correlating events across parties, and mentions client metadata documents and dynamic registration for learning about clients, but none of these is defined as a contact or escalation channel.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no contact field is defined (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Searched all sections for contact, escalation, abuse and operator details. No contact channel.
claims.section: Searched all sections for contact, escalation, abuse and operator details

claims.text: Audit logs are mandatory.
claims.quote: deployments MUST produce durable audit logs covering authorization decisions and subsequent remediations.

claims.text: Client metadata documents may describe clients.
claims.quote: Where supported, they MAY use Client ID Metadata Documents

rows.answer: Optional. Participants MAY exchange security events through the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, using CAEP for access changes and RISC for risk incidents (e.g. token replay suspected, risk elevated), and recipients SHOULD reduce access in response. The draft does not say who must send which events. Monitoring systems SHOULD also correlate events across agents, tools, services and models to detect misuse.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: signals between parties are named but optional; the calibration examples are red because they define none.

claims.text: Signals through SSF, CAEP or RISC.
claims.quote: Any participant in the system, including the Agent, Tool, System, LLM or other resources and service MAY subscribe to change notifications using eventing mechanisms such as the OpenID Shared Signals Framework {{SSF}}

claims.text: Recipients should remediate.
claims.quote: the recipient SHOULD remediate by attenuating access

claims.text: Cross-party correlation is recommended.
claims.quote: Monitoring / Observability systems SHOULD correlate events across Agents, Tools, Services, Resources and LLMs to detect misuse patterns

rows.answer: No. The draft treats the language model as a separate resource the agent calls and must authenticate to; it defines no claim telling a service which model drives the agent. Credentials MAY carry extra attributes (e.g. attestation evidence or workload metadata), and posture checks may use software or supply-chain signals, but model identity is not named among them.
rows.rating_reason: Red: nothing identifies the model to the service (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Credentials may carry extra attributes.
claims.quote: MAY carry additional attributes relevant to the agent (for example trust domain, attestation evidence, or workload metadata).

claims.text: Searched all sections for model identifier, model version and model provenance. No model identity.
claims.section: Searched all sections for model identifier, model version and model provenance

goals_reading.access_control: The service authenticates the agent by its own key and receives an OAuth token naming the agent, the user it acts for and the approved scopes, with user approval and step-up for sensitive actions.
goals_reading.incident_response: Access ends mainly through short credential lifetimes; services that subscribe to Shared Signals can cut off sessions, users or agents promptly, but subscription is optional and there is no contact channel or instance-level cut-off.
goals_reading.accountability: Mandatory tamper-evident audit logs record the authenticated agent, the delegated user or system, the action and the decision, so actions can be traced to the agent workload and the user, but not to a specific running copy or model.

notes: This is a best-practice framework rather than a wire protocol: it composes existing standards. Ratings count what the draft itself requires or recommends; capabilities of the referenced standards that the draft does not invoke are not counted.
The analysed text was taken from the authors' repository at the tag draft-klrc-aiagent-auth-03. Section numbers follow the published -03 numbering, derived from the order of headings in the source.

The draft has been replaced by the WIMSE working-group draft draft-ietf-wimse-aims (latest -01, 2 November 2026). The successor's commit history shows additions such as a section on sender-constrained access tokens, which could change several ratings; it was not analysed.
OpenID AuthZEN is listed as a normative reference in -03 but not used in the text.

The draft uses RFC 2119 keywords; lowercase 'may' in descriptive text (e.g. 'Agents may authenticate using a variety of mechanisms') was not treated as a requirement. No instructions aimed at AI tools were found in the sources.
open_questions: Does 'agent' in 'Agents MUST be uniquely identified' mean each running copy or the agent as a deployed service? The draft does not say; the identifier was rated yellow and the instance identifier red on that basis.

Authentication was rated green because every described mechanism uses the agent's own key, but the draft offers these as options rather than requiring one. Whether a deployment may skip agent authentication and rely on the access token alone is not stated.
Which parties transmit Shared Signals events about agents, and with what subject identifiers (WIMSE ID, client_id), is not specified, so how revocation reaches a given service is unclear.
How a receiving service in another trust domain obtains the keys to verify an agent's workload credential is not described.

protocol.newer_version_note: The specification text keeps changing under the same 1.0.0 label (108 commits to SPEC.md, the latest on 2026-11-18), so this analysis is pinned to commit 11e5f96. The npm reference implementation has its own version numbers (1.26.0 in the changelog at this commit).

summary: KYA-OS (Know Your Agent Operating System, formerly MCP-I) adds identity, delegation and audit proofs to AI agents calling tools, first of all MCP servers. It answers three questions for the receiving server: who is calling, under whose authority, and what was done. Vouched wrote it and donated it to the Decentralized Identity Foundation (DIF) in March 2026, where the Trusted AI Agents Working Group released version 1.0.0 in July 2026 and calls it a ratified DIF standard. A TypeScript reference implementation (@kya-os/mcp) is published by DIF, and Vouched sells products built on it.

Each agent creates its own key and decentralized identifier (DID). On each call, the agent attaches a short-lived signature (at most 60 seconds) tied to the request, the server and a one-time nonce. Authority comes from a chain of signed delegation credentials rooted at a Responsible Party, with scoped actions and caveats such as spending limits, revocable through status lists. If authority is missing, the server can send the user to a consent page. The server signs its responses for audit. KYA-OS leaves the choice of which roots to trust to each server, and defines no contact channel, cross-server signalling or model identity; an older session-based profile with weaker guarantees remains valid in 1.x.
how_it_works: Setup: the agent generates its own Ed25519 key pair and DID (did:key, or did:web published by its controller). The user or organisation that is accountable (the Responsible Party) signs a delegation credential naming the agent's key, with the allowed actions or scopes, caveats such as a maximum amount, an expiry and a revocation status entry; longer chains can re-delegate with narrower rights.

The agent calls a tool on a KYA-OS server. In the per-request profile it attaches a proof object signed with its key, covering a hash of the request, the server's DID as audience, a nonce and a validity window of at most 60 seconds, and may carry its delegation chain in the request metadata.
The server resolves the agent's DID document, checks that the key belongs to the DID, the audience, the request hash, the time window, that the nonce is new, and the signature.

The server then verifies the delegation chain: each hop's signature, that each hop narrows its parent, that the last delegate is the key that signed the request, that the root is one it trusts (if configured), that the invoked action is allowed, and that no hop is revoked in its issuer's status list.

If the delegation is missing or insufficient, the server returns a signed needs_authorization challenge with a consent URL; the user approves there, a new delegation credential is issued and the agent retries.
If all checks pass, the server runs the tool and returns the result with a signed response proof binding the request and response hashes and the delegation used, which both sides can keep for audit.

rows.short: DID identity, delegation chains and proofs for MCP agents
rows.answer: A DIF specification, first bound to MCP, where each agent signs every call with its own DID key and presents a revocable, scoped delegation chain rooted at an accountable party, so the server can check who is calling, under whose authority, and keep signed proofs of what was done.

claims.text: The specification's abstract.
claims.quote: KYA-OS enables MCP servers to verify who is calling (agent DID), what authority they hold (a delegation chain rooted at a Responsible Party, expressed as W3C Verifiable Credentials), and what was done (signed proof for audit trails).

claims.text: Every request carries its own proof in the per-request profile.
claims.quote: There is no session establishment and no handshake; every request carries its own proof.

rows.short: Agents calling MCP tools; downstream HTTP calls
rows.answer: Agents calling tools and resources on MCP servers, including across organisations, with delegated authority (e.g. payments within a limit). The proof and delegation chain travel in the MCP request metadata (_meta); outbound HTTP calls use KYA-OS headers; discovery uses Entity Cards projected onto MCP, A2A and NANDA metadata. The MCP server verifies itself (Level 2 and above) or an edge proxy verifies for legacy servers (Level 1), and gateways may pre-check headers.

claims.text: A layer that host protocols embed; MCP is the first binding.
claims.quote: KYA-OS is not a transport or a runtime, it is an identity and accountability layer that host protocols embed.

claims.text: Cross-organisational verification with a carried chain.
claims.section: 10.5 Carrying the chain with the request
claims.quote: This is the cross-organizational case: a resource server can verify an agent acting for an organization whose delegation records it cannot query.

claims.text: Edge proxy at Level 1, native verification at Level 2 and above.
claims.quote: At Conformance Level 2+, verification moves into the resource boundary (native server-side verification).

rows.short: Agent, Principal, Responsible Party, server, verifier, issuers
rows.answer: Agent: AI software identified by its own DID. Principal: whoever immediately delegates authority to the agent, typically the human operator. Responsible Party: the root issuer of the delegation chain, ultimately accountable (an organisation, or the Principal in personal use). MCP server or service: the resource being called, itself identified by a DID. Verifier: checks credentials, sometimes an edge proxy. Issuers: sign delegation, capability or identity-verification credentials. Registries (delegation, credential, trust) are optional indexes.

claims.text: Agent DID.
claims.quote: A Decentralized Identifier (DID) that uniquely identifies an AI agent.

claims.text: Principal.
claims.quote: The entity that immediately delegates authority to an agent — typically the human operator who launches the agent for a task.

claims.text: Responsible Party.
claims.quote: The entity ultimately accountable for the actions of an agent operating under a delegation chain.

claims.text: Verifier, often an edge proxy at Level 1.
claims.quote: At Conformance Level 1 (edge-proxy verification), the verifier sits in front of legacy MCP servers that don't natively understand KYA-OS.

claims.text: Registries.
claims.quote: The registry indexes anything addressable by DID — agents, MCP servers, services, and delegation policies.

rows.short: 1.0.0 Stable at DIF; Vouched's products implement it
rows.answer: Released. SPEC.md is version 1.0.0, marked Stable and described as ratified as a DIF standard; DIF and Vouched announced its release on 29 July 2026. The MCP extension binding is still a draft, and the text keeps changing under the 1.0.0 label. DIF publishes the reference implementation, and Vouched says its Know Your Agent product suite implements KYA-OS; no third-party deployment was found in a deployer's own source.

rows.short: DIDs, W3C VCs, ZCAP-LD, status lists, Ed25519 JWS
rows.answer: Decentralized Identifiers (did:key and did:web, optionally did:cheqd); W3C Verifiable Credentials (1.1 for the legacy delegation shape, 2.0 with ZCAP-LD capabilities for the newer profile); StatusList2021 and Bitstring Status List for revocation; Ed25519 (RFC 8032) signatures in JWS (RFC 7515), with ES256 allowed for request proofs; RFC 8785 JSON canonicalization; an optional RFC 9421 HTTP signature sibling; RFC 7638 thumbprints and DPoP-style cnf binding (RFC 9449); MCP 2026-07-28 and its OAuth hardening for the consent flow.

claims.text: DIDs, VCs, Ed25519 and StatusList2021.
claims.quote: The protocol uses Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) for agent identity, W3C Verifiable Credentials for delegation, Ed25519 signatures for cryptographic operations, and StatusList2021 for revocation.

claims.text: VC 2.0 with ZCAP-LD in the newer profile.

claims.section: 8.5 RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signature sibling (dual carrier)
claims.quote: A stock RFC 9421 verifier (SEP-1960, Cloudflare Web Bot Auth) reconstructs this base and verifies httpSig against the resolved DID key with zero new code.

rows.answer: Yes. Each agent is identified by a DID it controls: did:key (derived from its public key) or did:web (a document its controller publishes). The agent must generate its own key pair, and no registry or verifier may generate or hold it. In the per-request profile the proof names the caller's DID and key id, and the key must be listed in that DID's document. A did:web may be a persistent, organisation-hosted identity.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the identifier names the agent itself, with a key each agent generates (unlike the provider-level identifiers of all three calibration examples).

claims.text: The Agent DID identifies an AI agent.
claims.quote: A Decentralized Identifier (DID) that uniquely identifies an AI agent.

claims.text: Agents generate their own key pair.
claims.quote: An agent MUST generate its own keypair locally.

claims.text: Key generation on the agent's behalf is non-conformant.
claims.quote: Implementations that generate or hold agent secret keys on the agent's behalf are non-conformant.

claims.text: did:web is the persistent, organisation-hosted option.
claims.quote: Production servers, organizational identity

rows.answer: Partly. The recommended delegate is a fresh, single-purpose did:key minted per delegation, and every request proves possession of that key, so the server can tell one delegated agent instance from another. But this is a recommendation: an agent may use one persistent did:web across many delegations and running copies, and the legacy session profile allows anonymous sessions without an agent DID.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a per-instance key is the recommended model but not required, and a persistent DID may be shared by many running copies (all three calibration examples are red).

claims.text: Fresh key per delegation is RECOMMENDED.

claims.text: Possession is proven on every request.
claims.quote: Possession of that key is proven on every request

claims.text: did:web as an alternative durable name.

rows.short: Responsible Party DID, when delegation is used
rows.answer: Partly. When a call is authorized by delegation, the server recomputes the Responsible Party as the signed root issuer of the chain, and can see the Principal and every hop. That party is a DID, not necessarily a verified person or company: identity verification (KYC or KYB) can be attached as an optional credential. Delegation belongs to conformance Level 3, so servers at lower levels learn no principal.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: required (MUST) whenever a call is authorized by delegation, but delegation is only at conformance Level 3 or for gated tools, and identity verification of the party is optional (between Visa TAP's optional object and a required verified identity).

claims.text: Every chain ends at a Responsible Party.
claims.quote: Every chain MUST terminate at a Responsible Party.

claims.text: Delegation is Level 3.
claims.quote: Level 3 — Full Delegation: VC issuance/verification, delegation graphs, revocation, outbound propagation

claims.text: KYC/KYB as an optional credential on the Responsible Party.
claims.quote: KYC/KYB rides the same rail as an IdentityVerificationCredential on the responsibleParty, asserting the verification fact and level, never raw PII

claims.text: On success the verifier holds the recomputed Responsible Party.
claims.quote: On success the Verifier holds the recomputed responsibleParty, the leaf invoker, the leaf's granted actions, the chain depth

rows.answer: Yes. In the per-request profile every call carries a proof object signed with the agent's DID key (EdDSA or ES256), covering a hash of the request method and parameters, the server's DID as audience, a nonce, and created and expires times; it is proof of possession, so a captured credential is useless without the key. An RFC 9421 HTTP signature can be added. The delegation credentials are signed by their issuers. A server that gates a call rejects it without a proof; the older session profile, still valid in 1.x, works differently.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a verifiable, proof-of-possession credential on every gated request (stronger than the calibration examples, which are also green).

claims.text: Covered claims of the proof.
claims.quote: The covered claims are every proof field EXCEPT the two signatures (jws, httpSig), i.e. {prf, alg, did, kid, audience, nonce, created, expires, requestHash} plus cnf when present.

claims.text: Missing proof on a gated call is rejected.
claims.quote: a missing or stripped proof on a gated call is rejected by the proof gate (proof_missing, §5.2), regardless of what the declaration said;

claims.text: The per-request proof is the normative authority.
claims.quote: A conformant verifier MUST be able to authorize and audit a request from the proof and grant alone, with no server-side session state.

claims.text: Undeclared clients are processed as core MCP in optional mode.
claims.quote: A request from a client that did not declare the extension is processed as core MCP.

rows.answer: Very short for the request proof: expires minus created must not exceed 60 seconds, checked with about 5 seconds of clock skew, and verifiers reject a longer window (ttl_too_long) or an expired one; the nonce must be unseen. Delegation credentials carry their own expiry set by the issuer with no maximum, and short-lived delegations are recommended for high-stakes resources. Legacy sessions expire after 30 minutes idle by default.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a specific short maximum that verifiers must enforce (same colour as Visa TAP's 8-minute window).

claims.text: 60-second maximum.
claims.quote: and expires - created MUST NOT exceed 60 seconds

claims.text: Verifier check.
claims.quote: expires - created ≤ 60 (ttl_too_long)

claims.text: Short-lived delegations recommended for high-stakes resources.
claims.quote: Operators of high-stakes resources SHOULD reduce the race window by issuing short-lived delegations

rows.answer: Yes. The server resolves the caller's DID (did:key locally, did:web over HTTPS), checks that the key belongs to that DID, then checks the audience, the request hash, the time window, the nonce and the signature, failing closed on any error. Delegation hops are verified against their issuers' DID documents and status lists. No prior relationship with the agent is needed.
rows.rating_reason: Green: verifiable from published DID documents with expiry checks and no prior relationship (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: The key must be in the DID document.
claims.quote: the per-request proof's kid MUST resolve to a verification method of proof.did

claims.text: Audience check.
claims.quote: audience === expectedAudience, else audience_mismatch.

claims.text: A carried chain verifies without a registry or other out-of-band lookup.
claims.section: 10.5 Carrying the chain with the request
