rows.property: Authentication of the agent or user
rows.short: Yes, the agent's own key per request
rows.answer: Yes, for the agent. On each request the server verifies a signature made with the agent's own DID key, which the agent generated and no other party may hold, and the delegation only works for the key it names (the last delegate must equal the signer). The server does not authenticate the human user; the user appears as the signer of the delegation. The legacy session profile, still valid in 1.x, allows weaker modes such as anonymous sessions.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the service verifies per-request proof from a per-agent key (unlike all three calibration examples, which verify provider-level keys or tokens issued elsewhere); borderline because the legacy profile remains valid.

claims.text: Level 2+ authenticates the agent, but access rests on delegation.
claims.quote: Direct server-side verification (Conformance Level 2+) authenticates the agent's identity, but the access decision still rests on the delegation chain the agent presents

claims.text: Leaf join.
claims.quote: The leaf delegate equals proof.did (§10.2), else delegation_invalid.

claims.text: Legacy handshake allows anonymous sessions.
claims.quote: identityState: 'anonymous' | 'authenticated';

rows.answer: Yes. Delegation credentials carry scopes or allowed actions, an audience or invocation target, time bounds and caveats such as a maximum amount or a budget. Each re-delegation must be equal or narrower, every call must name the specific scope it uses, and the server rejects actions outside the leaf's grant. These checks are required whenever the server authorizes by delegation.
rows.rating_reason: Green: fine-grained permissions the service enforces (same colour as MCP Authorization's scopes).

claims.text: Attenuation at every hop.
claims.quote: A chain is valid only if EVERY hop attenuates its parent.

claims.text: Designation invariant.
claims.quote: An invocation that omits the specific resource designation MUST be rejected, even if the delegation would have authorized it under any matching scope.

claims.text: Action check.
claims.quote: The invoked action is in the leaf's allowedAction, else action_not_delegated.

rows.answer: Yes. When a call lacks a delegation or enough scope, the server returns a signed needs_authorization challenge with a consent URL and requested scopes; the user authenticates and grants authorization there, a delegation credential is issued, and the agent retries. The challenge is signed so the client can detect a swapped URL. Delegations can also be issued by an agent to a sub-agent, which is not a human approval.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the protocol defines a user approval step the service can trigger before access (same colour as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Server returns needs_authorization.
claims.quote: If delegation is missing or insufficient: return needs_authorization error

claims.text: The user grants authorization.
claims.quote: User authenticates and grants authorization

claims.text: Consent gating for actions needing explicit human approval.
claims.quote: Per-tool consent gating for actions that require explicit human approval.

rows.short: Responsible Party; which roots to trust is local
rows.answer: Partly. The Responsible Party at the root of the chain vouches for the agent by signing the delegation, and capability or KYC credentials from trusted issuers can add assurance. But which roots and issuers a server accepts is its own configuration: checking trusted roots applies only when configured, and trust-registry standing is advisory, not blocking. The protocol names no party that vets agents for all servers.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: vouching through the delegation root is defined, but whether a trusted party stands behind it depends on optional root pinning, optional KYC credentials and an advisory registry (between MCP Authorization's green and Web Bot Auth's red).

claims.text: Trusted roots are checked only when configured.
claims.quote: When the Verifier configures trusted root issuers, issuer(rootVC) is one of them, else delegation_invalid.

claims.text: Registry standing is advisory.
claims.quote: Trust-registry rejection is advisory, not blocking.

claims.text: The service decides who it trusts.
claims.quote: The service decides what scopes it accepts, who its trust registry trusts, and which did:web documents it will fetch.

rows.short: Yes, per delegation via status lists
rows.answer: Yes. Each delegation credential can carry a status list entry; the direct issuer, any ancestor or the Responsible Party can revoke it, and revocation cascades to every sub-delegation. Verifiers must fetch and verify the issuer's signed status list and reject revoked or unreadable entries; caches should be at most 60 seconds for high-privilege scopes, and the newer profile needs a live read for its top level. Access can be cut for one delegation, one agent key or a whole chain.
rows.rating_reason: Green: revocation is defined in the protocol, fine-grained and reaches the verifier through status lists within a bounded cache time (all three calibration examples are red).

claims.text: Root can revoke the whole chain.
claims.quote: The Responsible Party at the root of the chain. The root issuer MAY revoke the entire chain.

claims.text: Cascading revocation.
claims.quote: Recursively mark all descendant delegations as revoked

claims.text: Cache bound.

claims.text: Status checking is a Level 3 requirement.
claims.quote: Check credential status via StatusList2021

rows.answer: No. KYA-OS names the accountable Responsible Party by DID and keeps signed audit proofs, but defines no contact or escalation field for it or for the agent. A DID document could list service endpoints, but the specification does not define one for reports.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no contact field or process is defined (same as all three calibration examples).

claims.quote: Root-accountable Entity (§2.2, §10.2). SHOULD be did:web.

rows.answer: No. The specification describes a trust registry for checking standing and says reputation is tracked mainly on the Responsible Party, but defines no message or API for one service to report an agent to others. Delegation graphs and revocation state are not synchronised across deployments, and directory federation is out of scope for this version.

rows.answer: No. Identity is about the agent's key, its type and its accountable party. The legacy handshake allows optional, self-asserted client information (name, version, platform), and key custody may be hardware-attested, but nothing identifies the AI model.
rows.rating_reason: Red: nothing identifies the model (same as all three calibration examples).

goals_reading.access_control: A server can allow or refuse each call by the agent's own key and by a scoped, attenuated delegation chain, including spending caveats, and can ask the user for consent when authority is missing. Which delegation roots it accepts is its own configuration.
goals_reading.incident_response: Delegations can be revoked by the issuer, any ancestor or the Responsible Party, cascading to sub-delegations, and verifiers see it through status lists within about a minute for high-privilege scopes. There is no contact channel or way to warn other servers.
goals_reading.accountability: Each call can be traced to the agent's key, the delegation chain and its Responsible Party, and the server's signed response proofs and audit records bind what was requested and returned. The Responsible Party is a DID, linked to a verified person or organisation only if a KYC credential is attached.

notes: Name collisions: 'KYA' (Know Your Agent) is also used by unrelated work, e.g. the Open-KYA 'KYA Manifest Standard' (open-kya.github.io) and vendors' 'Know Your Agent' products. This analysis covers KYA-OS, formerly MCP-I, in the DIF repository decentralized-identity/kya-os-mcp. The spec also says it was 'previously known as MCP-Identity / MCP-I'.

Two profiles coexist in 1.x: a legacy session-bound profile (unsigned handshake, server-signed response proofs, StatusList2021 VC 1.1 delegations) and the per-request Entity Card profile (agent-signed proof on every call, VC 2.0 with ZCAP-LD). Ratings mostly follow the per-request profile, which SPEC.md section 5 calls the normative, durable authority; where the legacy profile is weaker, the answer says so.
Conformance has three separate ladders that reuse the names L1 to L3 (Core, Entity Card, Audit Assurance), which is easy to misread.
The specification uses RFC 2119 keywords. MAY* on the trust row reflects that trusted-root checking applies 'when the Verifier configures' it rather than a keyword.

The press release and Vouched page were checked with a web tool, which limits quotes to about 125 characters, so those quotes are sentence fragments. The DIF website and modelcontextprotocol-identity.io could not be fetched in this session; the GitHub repository was used as the primary source.

protocol.name: MCP Authorization
protocol.spec_version: MCP specification revision 2026-07-28 (Basic > Authorization)
protocol.maintainer: Model Context Protocol project (lead maintainers), under the Agentic AI Foundation
protocol.newer_version_note: 2026-07-28 is the current revision. A draft revision exists in the same repository and was not analysed.

summary: MCP Authorization is the security layer of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol that lets AI applications connect to outside tools and data through MCP servers. It answers one question for a remote MCP server: is this application allowed to call me on behalf of this user, and for what? Authorization is optional in MCP and covers only servers reached over HTTP, not local servers. The current version is the dated revision 2026-07-28, maintained by the MCP project, and it is supported by AI applications such as Claude's connectors.

It is a profile of OAuth 2.1, the widely used standard for delegated access on the web. The MCP server names its authorization server; the AI application sends the user there to sign in and approve access, and receives an access token that only works at that one server and only for the approved scopes (permissions). The token is sent with every request and the server checks it. The server therefore learns that the request is approved, but not which agent instance or AI model is behind it. MCP itself defines no way to revoke access or to contact the application's operator, and the token is a bearer token, so whoever holds it can use it.
how_it_works: The AI application (the MCP client) calls the MCP server without a token and receives a 401 response that points to the server's protected resource metadata (RFC 9728).
From that metadata the client finds the server's authorization server and identifies itself with a client ID, ideally an HTTPS URL to a Client ID Metadata Document describing the application.
The client opens the authorization server in the user's browser. The user signs in and approves the requested scopes; PKCE protects this exchange.
The authorization server issues an access token for that specific MCP server (using a resource indicator, RFC 8707).
The client sends the token as a bearer token on every request. The MCP server checks that it is valid, unexpired and issued for it, and answers 401 (invalid token) or 403 (missing scope) otherwise.

rows.answer: An OAuth access token, sent as a bearer token in the Authorization header of every HTTP request. It is issued by the server's authorization server for that specific MCP server, and can be a signed JWT or an opaque string, as the authorization server decides. A bearer token is not bound to the client, so anyone who obtains it can use it. Proof-of-possession binding (e.g. DPoP or mTLS) is not part of the specification.

protocol.name: OAuth 2.0 AI Agent Instance Profile
protocol.spec_version: draft-mcguinness-oauth-ai-agent-instance-00
protocol.maintainer: Karl McGuinness (independent), individual Internet-Draft aimed at the IETF OAuth working group
protocol.newer_version_note: -00 is the only revision submitted to the IETF. The author's repository README (14 September 2026) marks it superseded and not being progressed, replaced by an agent federation profile together with Client Instance Identification (draft-mcguinness-oauth-client-instance-id). The successors were not analysed.

summary: Many AI agent platforms register one OAuth client and run thousands of agent sessions under it, so a service receiving their access tokens sees only the platform, never the specific agent. The OAuth 2.0 AI Agent Instance Profile tries to fix this by giving each running agent instance its own attested identifier and carrying it into the access tokens that services receive. It is aimed at agent platforms, authorization servers and the APIs or MCP servers they call. It is an individual Internet-Draft by Karl McGuinness, version -00 from July 2026, with no named deployments, and the author has since marked it superseded and not being progressed.

It is a profile of a companion draft, the OAuth 2.0 Client Instance Assertion. An Agent Attester (usually the platform's control plane) signs evidence naming the instance (agent_instance_id), optionally its platform, model and runtime, and binds it to a key the instance holds. The authorization server checks this evidence and issues an access token that names the user in sub and the agent instance in act.sub, and that is bound to the instance's key (DPoP or mutual TLS, never a bearer token). Sub-agents get nested act chains through token exchange. The profile leaves agent permissions, contact channels and signals between services out, and its model claims are only as reliable as the Attester.
how_it_works: The agent platform registers its OAuth client for the profile (ai_agent_instance_profile set to true) and names its Agent Attester, either in its instance_issuers client metadata or by agreement with an authorization server that trusts that Attester.

When the platform starts an agent instance (a session, task or runtime), the Agent Attester mints signed evidence for it: a unique agent_instance_id, optional agent_platform, agent_model and agent_runtime claims, and a cnf claim binding a key that only this instance holds.

The instance asks the authorization server for a token (e.g. redeeming an authorization code after the user approved the client), presenting the evidence and a DPoP proof. The authorization server checks the signature, the client binding, replay and possession of the bound key.

The authorization server issues a sender-constrained access token: sub names the user, act.sub names the agent instance with sub_profile ai_agent, and the model may be surfaced if local policy allows. For a self-acting agent the instance itself is sub.

The instance calls the resource server (e.g. an MCP server) with the token and a fresh proof of possession. The resource server validates both and can key policy, rate limits and audit records on the instance, not only on the platform.

If the instance spawns a sub-agent, the sub-agent exchanges the token while presenting its own evidence, producing a nested act chain. If an instance misbehaves, the authorization server can revoke all tokens for that one instance.

rows.answer: An OAuth profile in which an attester signs an identifier for each running AI agent instance, so that the access tokens a service receives name that specific instance (and optionally its model), bound to a key only that instance holds.

rows.answer: AI agent platforms (hosted orchestrators, and also command-line or desktop agents) that call APIs or MCP servers through OAuth. The identity travels inside the OAuth access token, which the resource server validates itself on each request. The authorization server does most of the work: it checks the Attester's evidence at its token endpoint and decides what goes into the token.

rows.answer: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) with JWTs (RFC 7519). The companion draft OAuth 2.0 Client Instance Assertion (CIA-CORE) supplies token-endpoint processing, key binding, token format and revocation. Token Exchange (RFC 8693) provides the act claim for delegation chains; DPoP (RFC 9449) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705) bind tokens to a key. Attestation-Based Client Authentication (an OAuth working-group draft) is an alternative carrier, Entity Attestation Token (RFC 9711) carries runtime evidence, and the OAuth Entity Profiles draft supplies the ai_agent label.

protocol.name: Poppy
protocol.spec_version: Personal Agent Protocol 1.0 (published, frozen), repository commit 589743a
protocol.maintainer: Sierra (spec authors), developed with Meta and design partners; published on GitHub under Apache 2.0
protocol.newer_version_note: A 1.1 draft is in progress in the same repository and was not analysed. Version 1.0 has not changed since it was frozen on 2026-11-14 (commit 8c02b42).

summary: Personal Agent Protocol, known as Poppy, defines how a person's own AI agent (e.g. Meta's Muse) works with a company on that person's behalf: finding what the company offers, identifying itself, signing the person in, and using the company's APIs, website or company agent. It aims to replace today's all-or-nothing choice, in which agents either pass as the user or are blocked. Sierra leads the work with Meta and more than 100 design partners, and publishes it openly on GitHub under Apache 2.0, outside any standards body. Version 1.0 was published on 14 November 2026. Meta's Muse supports it, and Sierra says Shopify has enabled it for every merchant.

Every request carries a Session JWT, signed for that one request with a short-lived delegated key, that names the agent (its client_id, the URL of its metadata document), a pseudonymous User ID that differs at every company, and the Session. Account access is plain OAuth: the person signs in and approves scopes on the company's own page, and the agent then sends an access token alongside the Session JWT. Extensions add approval of an action's exact terms, a link to UCP for checkout, and a transitional sign-in with the user's password. Poppy does not identify individual agent instances or the AI model, defines no contact channel or warnings between companies, and leaves the choice of which agents to accept to each company.
how_it_works: Setup: the Company publishes /.well-known/poppy.json listing its channels (APIs, website, Company Agent) and, if it offers sign-in, points to its OAuth issuer and scopes. The Personal Agent's operator publishes a client metadata document at an HTTPS URL, which is its client_id, with its public keys (jwks_uri).

For each request, the Personal Agent signs a Session JWT with a short-lived delegated key, vouched for by a delegation signed with a key from its jwks_uri. The JWT names the Personal Agent, a pairwise User ID, the Session, the method and URL, and goes in the Poppy-Session header. A Web Bot Auth operator signature is recommended on top.

The Company, or a gateway in front of it, fetches the client metadata and keys, verifies the delegation and signature, the audience, method, URL and freshness, and then starts or continues a signed-out Session for that pseudonymous User.

When a task needs the User's account, the Personal Agent sends the User to the Company's own sign-in and consent page (Direct Sign-In, or Device Sign-In with a code). The User approves some or all of the requested scopes, and the Personal Agent exchanges the result for access and refresh tokens, authenticating with a client assertion.

Signed-in requests carry the access token together with the Session JWT, whose ath claim binds the two. The Company checks the token, its scopes and that both belong to the same client_id, then decides. With the Operations extension, a consequential action first returns its exact terms, which the User, or the agent on the User's instruction, approves before the Company performs it.
To end access, the Personal Agent revokes its refresh tokens (sign-out), or the User disconnects it in the Company's account settings; the Company can also refuse a client_id altogether.

rows.short: Personal agents sign each request; users sign in via OAuth
rows.answer: An open protocol, led by Sierra with Meta, where a person's AI agent signs every request to a company with a per-request Session JWT naming itself and a pseudonymous user, and gets account access through OAuth sign-in on the company's own page.

rows.short: Personal agents at companies: APIs, web, chat
rows.answer: Consumer personal agents doing tasks at companies (e.g. shopping, bookings, account changes) through the company's APIs (OpenAPI or MCP), its website, or conversations with the company's own agent. Identity travels in HTTP headers: a signed Session JWT and, once signed in, an OAuth access token. The company's application or a gateway in front of it verifies them, and an optional Web Bot Auth signature lets CDNs and bot defenses recognise the operator earlier.

Company: an entity that implements the protocol so Personal Agents can work with it, with its own OAuth issuer when it offers sign-in. rows.short: OAuth 2.0, CIMD, JWT, DPoP, RFC 9421, RFC 9474
rows.answer: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) following the security best practice RFC 9700, with PKCE (RFC 7636), device grant (RFC 8628), RFC 9207, RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 metadata, RFC 7009 revocation, RFC 8707 resource indicators and optional PAR (RFC 9126). Agent identity uses Client ID Metadata Documents (an IETF draft) and private_key_jwt (RFC 7523). Session JWTs reuse DPoP ideas (RFC 9449), with delegated keys (RFC 7800, RFC 7638) and optional RSA blind signatures (RFC 9474); operator signatures use RFC 9421 and the Web Bot Auth draft. APIs are OpenAPI or MCP.

claims.quote: A Company can ask Personal Agents to tell it when a User's task can't be done through this protocol.

rows.answer: No. Poppy defines no way for one Company to warn others about a misbehaving Personal Agent. Pairwise User IDs and per-Company delegated keys are designed so Companies cannot match a User across Companies.
rows.rating_reason: Red: not addressed (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Searched the specification, extensions and guides for reputation, shared signals, abuse reports and events between Companies. None is defined.
User IDs are designed against cross-Company matching.
claims.quote: It is opaque and different for each Company, so Companies can't match Users with each other.

rows.answer: No. The Company learns the Personal Agent's client_id and display name, and in conversations each message says whether a person or an AI wrote it, but no field names the AI model or its version.
rows.rating_reason: Red: nothing identifies the model (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Human or AI marking in conversations.
claims.quote: Both sides say whether a person or an AI is taking part.

claims.text: Searched client metadata (4.1), Session JWT claims (5.2), message fields (8.4) and agent context (9.4) for model, version or attestation. None is defined.

goals_reading.access_control: A Company can let accepted Personal Agents use signed-out APIs and pages, and gate account actions by OAuth scopes the User approves on its own page, with per-action approval of exact terms through the Operations extension. Which agents it accepts is its own policy, outside the protocol.
goals_reading.incident_response: The Company can revoke refresh tokens per account and Personal Agent, the User can disconnect an agent in account settings, and the Company can refuse a client_id, which cuts off every User of that Personal Agent. One agent instance cannot be cut off, and a delegated key stays usable until its delegation expires (up to 24 hours).
goals_reading.accountability: Every verified request names the Personal Agent (client_id), a stable pseudonymous User, the Session and optionally an Agent ID, and signed-in requests name the Company's own account. Approvals can carry a reference to the operator's record, but the AI model and an operator contact are not identified.

notes: The specification uses RFC 2119 keywords in capitals; requirement levels in this analysis follow those capitals.

Version 1.0 was announced by Sierra and Meta on 13 November 2026; the repository marked it published and froze it on 14 November 2026 (commit 8c02b42). Some third-party pages still call it 'draft 1.0', and the repository README still says the site publishes a draft specification; the 1.0 page itself says 'This is version 1.0.'
Venue is set to 'vendor': the specification is written in a repository run by Sierra, with Meta and design partners contributing feedback, and no standards body or foundation governs it.
The guides are non-normative recommendations; claims quoted from them are marked as guidance in the answers.
The repository contains AGENTS.md files with instructions aimed at AI coding tools (for contributors editing the site). They were treated as data and not followed.
Name collision: 'PAP' is also the PPP Password Authentication Protocol (RFC 1334), which is unrelated. poppy.md is an unofficial third-party site and was not used as a source.
Quotes from sierra.ai, muse.ai and about.fb.com were checked with a web tool (WEB-OK) because those sites could not be downloaded by script from this environment.
open_questions: Shopify's enablement for every merchant is stated by Sierra; no Shopify documentation was found that says what Shopify's poppy.json files offer (signed-out Sessions only, sign-in, UCP extension).
How many Companies actually verify the Session header (a SHOULD) rather than ignoring it, and how short their acceptance windows are.
Whether Muse sends an Agent ID, and whether it uses blind signing or holds delegated keys on Meta's servers.
Whether Companies invalidate access tokens at sign-out in practice, which decides how quickly revocation takes effect.

The spec says the Company is identified by its domain; it does not say how a Personal Agent operator's keys used for Web Bot Auth relate to its client_id beyond 'a shared origin alone does not establish' the link.

protocol.name: Transaction Tokens For Agents
protocol.full_name: Transaction Tokens For Agents (draft-araut-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents), an extension of OAuth Transaction Tokens
protocol.spec_version: draft-araut-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-03, building on draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-11
protocol.maintainer: Ashay Raut (individual Internet-Draft); the base Transaction Tokens draft is maintained by the IETF OAuth working group (editors from CrowdStrike, Practical Identity and Defakto Security)
protocol.newer_version_note: -03 is the latest revision. Earlier versions were published as draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-00 to -06 before the April 2026 rename. For the base draft, -11 is the latest revision; its repository already holds later edits from working-group last call that were not analysed.

summary: Inside a company's systems, one request often passes through many internal services, and when an AI agent started it, the services deep in that chain usually cannot tell. OAuth Transaction Tokens, an IETF OAuth working-group draft, already give each internal service a short-lived signed token describing who the transaction is for and what it is for. Transaction Tokens For Agents is an individual draft by Ashay Raut (version -03, October 2026) that adds agent context to those tokens, so internal services can tell agent-driven calls from direct human calls and audit them. No deployment is named.

A single Transaction Token Service in the trust domain issues the tokens. The extension adds an agentic_ctx claim naming the agent that started the chain and the agent at the current hop, a hop count, and an optional minimum assurance level, and fixes how the user (sub) and the delegated agent (act) are carried. Each time an agent hands work on, it gets a replacement token: identity stays fixed, the hop count rises and permissions can only shrink. The tokens are bearer-style and stay inside one trust domain. Neither draft defines revocation, contact channels, model identity or a way for services to warn each other.
how_it_works: A user asks an agent to do a task (or the agent starts on a schedule). The agent obtains an ordinary OAuth access token, through an authorization code flow for a user or client credentials when autonomous, and calls the trust domain's external endpoint (e.g. an API gateway).

The gateway sends that access token and its own credentials to the Transaction Token Service in an OAuth token-exchange request, asking for a Transaction Token with a narrow scope for this transaction.

The Transaction Token Service authenticates the gateway, validates the access token, checks (e.g. by looking up the client_id in an Agent Attribute Store) whether the caller is an agent, and issues a short-lived signed token: sub (the user, or the agent itself), act copied from the access token, scope, a transaction ID (txn) and agentic_ctx (proximate and originating agent, hop count 1).

Each internal service receives the token in the Txn-Token HTTP header, checks its signature, trust-domain audience and expiry, and applies its own policy (e.g. restrict agent chains, or refuse beyond a hop limit).

When an internal agent takes over and calls further services, it asks for a replacement token: sub, act, txn and the originating agent stay fixed, the proximate agent changes, the hop count rises, and scope and assurance level can only go down.
The Transaction Token Service logs each issuance and replacement, so the full agent chain for a transaction ID can be reconstructed after an incident.

sources.title: Transaction Tokens, draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens-11 (OAuth working group, base specification)

rows.short: Agent chain context inside internal Transaction Tokens
rows.answer: An individual-draft extension of OAuth Transaction Tokens: inside one trust domain, the Transaction Token Service adds an agentic_ctx claim naming the originating and current agent, a hop count and an optional minimum assurance level, so every internal service in a call chain can see that agents were involved.

claims.text: The extension defines agentic_ctx.
claims.quote: The extension defines the `agentic_ctx` claim, a structured JWT claim that carries chain-level metadata required for multi-agent flow integrity.

claims.text: Downstream workloads use Transaction Tokens for authorization.
claims.quote: Downstream workloads use Txn-tokens to apply authorization decisions based on this context within a specific transaction.

rows.short: Internal call chains within one trust domain
rows.answer: Internal service chains inside one organisation's trust domain (e.g. microservices and data stores) when a request was started by an AI agent, either an outside agent entering through an API gateway or internal agents handing work to each other. The token travels in its own Txn-Token HTTP header and every internal workload verifies it itself. It must not be accepted outside its trust domain; the base draft points to Identity and Authorization Chaining for crossing domains.

claims.text: Typical chains start with a third-party agent and pass through internal agents.
claims.quote: In complex agentic workflows, a transaction often originates from a 3rd-party (3P) agent and propagates through one or more 1st-party (1P) agents within the local trust domain.

claims.text: Tokens travel in a dedicated HTTP header.
claims.quote: A workload that invokes another workload using HTTP and needs to present a Txn-Token to the invoked workload MUST use the HTTP Header "Txn-Token" to communicate the Txn-Token in the HTTP Request.

claims.text: Tokens are bound to one trust domain.
claims.quote: A Txn-Token MUST NOT be accepted outside the Trust Domain identified by the `aud` claim.

claims.text: Crossing trust domains uses Identity Chaining.
claims.section: 14. Preserving transaction context across Trust Domains
claims.quote: it SHOULD use OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains {{I-D.ietf-oauth-identity-chaining}}.

rows.short: Agent, gateway, Token Service, Attribute Store, workloads
rows.answer: Human subject: the user who starts a task (absent in autonomous flows). Agent application: external (3P) or internal (1P), split into an inference layer that runs the model and an infrastructure layer that handles tokens. External endpoint: the published interface (e.g. an API gateway) that first receives the request. Transaction Token Service (TTS): issues and replaces tokens, one per trust domain. Agent Attribute Store: a logical role recording which workloads are agents and their attributes. Workloads and resource servers: receive and check tokens.

claims.text: Definition of the Transaction Token Service.
claims.quote: A special service within the Trust Domain that issues Txn-Tokens to requesting workloads.

claims.text: Definition of the Agent Attribute Store.
claims.quote: A logical role — not a defined protocol interface — that MAY be realized as an agent registry, service catalog, policy engine, or any equivalent mechanism accessible within the trust domain.

claims.text: Definition of the external endpoint.
claims.quote: A published interface to a Trust Domain that results in the invocation of a workload within the Trust Domain.

claims.text: Definition of the inference layer.
claims.quote: The component of an agent system that runs the AI model (e.g., an LLM), processes inputs, generates plans, and produces tool calls or outputs.

claims.text: Definition of the infrastructure layer.
claims.quote: The component of an agent system that executes tool calls, manages network I/O, enforces security policies, and interacts with external services including the Transaction Token Service.

rows.answer: Early proposal. The extension is an individual, Informational Internet-Draft at version -03 (31 October 2026), not adopted by a working group; it was first published in November 2025 under the name draft-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents. Its base, Transaction Tokens, is an OAuth working-group draft at -11 and not yet an RFC. No named deployment of the agent extension was found.
rows.rating_reason: Red: an individual draft with no named deployments, built on a base that is itself still a draft.

claims.text: Document name and revision.
claims.quote: docname: draft-araut-oauth-transaction-tokens-for-agents-03

claims.text: The base draft is a working-group document.
claims.quote: wg: oauth

claims.text: Searched all sections of both drafts, and the web for agentic_ctx implementations; no implementation or deployment is named.

rows.answer: OAuth Transaction Tokens (draft-ietf-oauth-transaction-tokens) is the base: it defines the token, its claims, the Transaction Token Service and the Txn-Token header. Tokens are requested through OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), which also defines the act claim the extension reuses. Tokens are JWTs (RFC 7519) signed with JWS (RFC 7515); incoming access tokens follow RFC 9068; the transaction ID comes from Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417). The extension defines no new token or grant types.

claims.text: The extension reuses act and sub.
claims.quote: It does not define new token types or grant types; it operates entirely within the existing Transaction Token issuance and replacement mechanisms defined by the base specification.

claims.text: Token requests use RFC 8693.
claims.quote: If the transaction token request is made via HTTP to a remote server, it MUST use {{RFC8693}} as described in this specification.

claims.text: Tokens are JWS-signed JWTs.
claims.quote: A Txn-Token is a JSON Web Token {{RFC7519}} protected by a JSON Web Signature {{RFC7515}}.

claims.text: The txn claim comes from RFC 8417.
claims.quote: REQUIRED A unique transaction identifier as defined in Section 2.2 of {{RFC8417}}.

rows.short: Agent ID from act.sub or client_id
rows.answer: Partly, and only when the caller is recognised as an agent. The Transaction Token Service then adds agentic_ctx with proximate_agent.id (the agent at the current hop) and originator.id (the agent that started the chain). The value comes from the access token's act.sub, an Agent Attribute Store lookup or the OAuth client_id, in that order, so it names the agent as a client or registered agent, shared by all its running copies. How agents are recognised is left to each deployment.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: the identifier names the agent application or client, shared by its instances (same as MCP Authorization), and the claim carrying it is optional.

claims.text: Where the agent identifier comes from.
claims.quote: At initial issuance, the TTS sets this field to the agent identifier derived from the access token (via `act.sub`, Agent Attribute Store lookup, or `client_id` — in that priority order).

claims.text: agentic_ctx is optional overall.
claims.quote: The Txn-Token MAY contain an `agentic_ctx` claim.

claims.text: It is mandatory once the caller is identified as a registered agent.
claims.quote: The TTS MUST populate the `agentic_ctx` claim with at minimum the normative fields defined in Section 3.6.1.

claims.text: Agent identification is deployment-defined.
claims.quote: The specific mechanism for agent identification is deployment-defined.

rows.answer: Partly. agentic_ctx can carry an optional session_id for the current and for the originating agent, identifying that agent's session as known to its own runtime (e.g. assigned by its framework or SDK). The value is self-asserted by the agent's infrastructure and unverified, and services and the Transaction Token Service must not use it for authorization. Its purpose is correlation: matching a transaction to the agent team's own logs during an investigation.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a per-session identifier for the running agent is defined but optional and unverified; the calibration examples are red because they define none. Red could be argued because the value is self-asserted (see open questions).

claims.text: session_id identifies the agent's runtime session.
claims.quote: A string identifying the session of the proximate agent as known to that agent's own runtime or infrastructure

claims.text: It is self-asserted.
claims.quote: This field is self-asserted by the agent's infrastructure layer and is therefore informational only.

claims.text: It must not be used for authorization.
claims.quote: Resource Servers and the TTS MUST NOT use this field as an authorization criterion.

claims.text: It is unverified.
claims.quote: Because these fields cannot be verified by the TTS or Resource Servers, a malicious agent could report a fabricated or another session's identifier.

rows.answer: Yes. Every Transaction Token must carry sub, the principal of the transaction: the user in a user-initiated flow, or typically the agent itself when it runs autonomously. When the original access token shows delegation, its act claim (the agent acting for the user) is copied into the token and can never be changed along the chain. The sub value is unique within the trust domain; its format is up to the Transaction Token Service.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the principal is a required claim the service receives in every token; MCP Authorization is red because it defines none.

claims.text: sub is required and names the principal.
claims.quote: REQUIRED This claim represents the principal of the transaction as defined by Section 4.1.2 of {{RFC7519}}.

claims.text: In autonomous flows sub usually names the agent.
claims.quote: For autonomous agents, the `sub` claim is determined based on the `subject_token` provided in the request, which typically represents the agent's own identity.

claims.text: act is copied from the access token.
claims.quote: If the access token contains an `act` claim, the Txn-Token Service copies the `act` claim value to the Txn-Token's `act` field.

claims.text: act is immutable.
claims.section: 3.3.1. Replacement When Caller is Identified as an Agent
claims.quote: The `act` claim is immutable throughout the entire transaction lifetime.

rows.short: Signed JWT in Txn-Token header, not bound
rows.answer: A Transaction Token: a short-lived JWT signed by the Transaction Token Service, sent in its own Txn-Token HTTP header (not the Authorization header) on each call between workloads. The signature covers all claims (subject, scope, transaction ID, context and agentic_ctx), so they cannot be altered along the chain. It is not bound to the sender: the base draft says it is not resistant to replay, and it must not be used to authenticate a workload.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a defined credential on every call that the service can verify; the answer notes it is not proof of possession (as for MCP Authorization's bearer token).

claims.text: Dedicated header is mandatory.
claims.quote: A workload that invokes another workload using HTTP and needs to present a Txn-Token to the invoked workload MUST use the HTTP Header "Txn-Token" to communicate the Txn-Token in the HTTP Request.

claims.text: Tokens are signed for integrity.
claims.quote: Txn-Tokens are cryptographically signed to ensure integrity.

claims.text: No replay resistance.
claims.quote: A Txn-Token is not resistant to replay attacks.

claims.text: Not an authentication credential.
claims.section: 13.12. Transaction Tokens Are Not Authentication Credentials
claims.quote: A workload MUST NOT use a transaction token to authenticate itself to another workload, service or the TTS.

rows.answer: Short, but with no enforced maximum. The base draft expects tokens to live on the order of minutes or less and says their lifetime MUST be kept short; every receiving workload must reject expired tokens. There is no maximum for verifiers to enforce, and the Transaction Token Service may issue replacement tokens that outlive the input token if its policy allows. The agent extension only adds that implementations must enforce strict lifetime validation.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a short lifetime is required of the issuer but stated only as 'on the order of minutes', with no maximum that verifiers must enforce; lower than Visa TAP's green (8-minute verifier rule), chosen under the tie rule.

claims.text: Expected lifetime is minutes or less.
claims.quote: Txn-Tokens are expected to be short-lived (on the order of minutes or less), and as a result MUST be used only for the expected duration of an external or internal invocation.

claims.text: Lifetime must be kept short.
claims.quote: For this reason, a Txn-Token lifetime MUST be kept short and follow the guidance given in {{txn-token-lifetime}}.

claims.text: Replacement can extend lifetime.
claims.quote: MAY issue a replacement Txn-Token with a lifetime exceeding the lifetime of the input Txn-Token, subject to the policy of the TTS.

claims.text: The extension requires strict lifetime validation.
claims.quote: Implementations MUST enforce strict token lifetime validation.

rows.answer: Yes, within the trust domain. Each receiving workload must check the token's signature, that its aud claim names the workload's own trust domain, and that it has not expired; the agent extension repeats that services must verify the signature before using any claim. The token is signed by the domain's single Transaction Token Service, whose signing keys are often known in advance; how they are distributed is not specified.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the service validates the token against its own trust domain's issuer with expiry checks (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Signature check is mandatory.
claims.quote: Validate the Txn-Token JWS signature.

claims.text: Audience check is mandatory.
claims.quote: Verify the `aud` claim identifies the Trust Domain of the workload.

claims.text: Expiry check is mandatory.
claims.quote: Verify the Txn-Token is not expired.

claims.text: The extension repeats the signature requirement.
claims.quote: Services MUST verify the cryptographic signature of every Txn-Token before processing its claims.

claims.text: Signing keys are often known in advance.
claims.quote: is not required as Txn-Tokens are bound to a single Trust Domain as defined by the `aud` claim and often the signing keys are known.

rows.property: Authentication of the agent or user
rows.short: No, checks a token issued by the TTS
rows.answer: No. A receiving service checks a token issued by the Transaction Token Service, and the base draft forbids using these tokens to authenticate a workload. The Transaction Token Service authenticates the workload that requests each token, and the extension requires mutually authenticated channels between components, but these authenticate the immediate caller (often a gateway), which the drafts do not link to the agent named in agentic_ctx. The user signs in at the original OAuth authorization server, outside this protocol.
rows.rating_reason: Red: the service only checks a token issued elsewhere, and channel authentication covers the immediate caller rather than the agent (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: Tokens are not authentication credentials.
claims.section: 13.12. Transaction Tokens Are Not Authentication Credentials
claims.quote: A workload MUST NOT use a transaction token to authenticate itself to another workload, service or the TTS.

claims.text: The TTS authenticates the requesting workload.
claims.quote: The TTS MUST authenticate the requesting workload before issuing or replacing a Txn-Token, using the access token presented in the exchange request.

claims.text: Channels between components are mutually authenticated.
claims.quote: All component communications MUST use mutually authenticated, encrypted channels (e.g., TLS with certificate validation).

claims.text: User sign-in happens in an ordinary OAuth flow before the protocol.
claims.quote: The agent application authenticates using an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow

claims.text: Searched 3.5 Agentic Context, 3.6 Agent Identification and 5.8 Infrastructure Security for a rule tying the caller's channel identity to proximate_agent.id: No link between the channel identity and agentic_ctx.
claims.section: Searched 3.5 Agentic Context, 3.6 Agent Identification and 5.8 Infrastructure Security for a rule tying the caller's channel identity to proximate_agent.id

rows.answer: Yes. Every token carries a required scope describing the narrow purpose of the transaction, and usually a tctx object with immutable transaction details (e.g. action, ticker and quantity of a trade). Scope can only be narrowed when a token is replaced, never widened, and the extension adds a hop count that services should check against a maximum. Scope values and how each service turns them into a decision are left to the deployment.
rows.rating_reason: Green: scoped permissions are required in every token and the service can enforce them (same as MCP Authorization).

claims.text: scope is a required claim.
claims.quote: REQUIRED The scope claim is defined in {{Section 4.2 of RFC8693}}.

claims.text: scope is the narrow purpose of the transaction.
claims.quote: The `scope` claim captures, as narrowly as possible, the purpose of this particular transaction.

claims.text: tctx carries immutable transaction details.
claims.quote: RECOMMENDED A JSON object that contains values that remain immutable throughout the Call Chain.

claims.text: Scope can only be attenuated.
claims.quote: Implementations MUST enforce the `scope` attenuation rules defined in Section 3.4.1, ensuring agent operations cannot exceed the scopes granted at initial token issuance.

claims.text: Services should check the hop count.
claims.quote: Resource Servers SHOULD evaluate this value against deployment-defined maximum hop limits when making authorization decisions.

claims.text: The decision itself is left to the service.
claims.quote: How the workload determines this authorization is out of scope for this specification.

rows.answer: No. The protocol has no approval step; it addresses agents that act across multi-step workflows without human oversight at each step. In the user-initiated flow the agent first gets an ordinary OAuth access token through an authorization code flow, where the user may consent, but that happens at the authorization server, before and outside the token exchange. The only approval the extension mentions is by software: the agent's infrastructure layer must check model output before using it in a token request.
rows.rating_reason: Red: any user approval happens outside the protocol (same as Visa TAP).

claims.text: Agents act without per-step human oversight.
claims.quote: AI agents operate autonomously across multi-step workflows, making tool calls and accessing data stores without direct human oversight at each step.

claims.text: User sign-in is an earlier OAuth flow.
claims.quote: The agent application authenticates using an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow

claims.text: Approval of model output is by the infrastructure layer.
claims.quote: The LLM's output MUST NOT be used as direct input to Txn-Token exchange requests without validation and approval by the infrastructure layer.

rows.short: The trust domain's Transaction Token Service
rows.answer: The trust domain's Transaction Token Service. There is exactly one logical service per trust domain; it decides which workloads may obtain tokens and with what content, and services accept only tokens signed for their domain. With the extension it also decides which callers count as agents, usually through an Agent Attribute Store whose posture and provenance attributes must come from the domain's deployment pipelines, not from the agents. Outside agents get only the context the domain's policy allows for unverified external actors.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the protocol names the party whose tokens services rely on (as MCP Authorization names the authorization server); the answer notes external agents are treated as unverified.

claims.text: One TTS per trust domain.
claims.quote: Each Trust Domain using Txn-Tokens MUST have exactly one logical TTS.

claims.text: The TTS decides who gets tokens.
claims.quote: A TTS should be selective in which workloads can successfully request a Txn-Token.

claims.text: Attribute Store contents must not come from agents.
claims.quote: These richer attributes are populated and maintained by the trust domain's deployment pipelines and MUST NOT be sourced from agent self-assertion.

claims.text: External agents get policy-limited context.
claims.quote: assigns context commensurate with the trust domain's policy for unverified external actors.

rows.answer: No. Neither draft defines a way to revoke a Transaction Token or an agent's access; the base draft relies on short lifetimes instead. Before issuing a token, the Transaction Token Service MAY check whether the presented access token was invalidated (e.g. through RFC 7662 introspection), which stops new tokens but not ones already issued, and it must not replace an expired token. The session_id helps an agent's owning team find the session for debugging or revocation, outside the protocol.
rows.rating_reason: Red: revocation is not defined (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Searched both drafts for revocation, revoke, invalidate and blocklist: No revocation mechanism.
claims.section: Searched both drafts for revocation, revoke, invalidate and blocklist

claims.text: The TTS may check if the access token was invalidated.
claims.quote: a TTS MAY, based on the risk profile of the deployment or transaction, verify whether the presented access token was invalidated.

claims.text: Expired tokens cannot be replaced.
claims.quote: MUST NOT issue a new Txn-Token when the Txn-Token being replaced has expired.

claims.text: session_id supports out-of-band revocation.
claims.quote: enabling that team to locate the corresponding session in their own runtime logs for debugging or revocation.

rows.short: No contact field; txn for correlation
rows.answer: No. Neither draft defines a contact or escalation field. The extension expects a workload that sees unexpected behaviour to share the transaction ID (txn) and session_id with the agent's owning team, and the Transaction Token Service operator can supply the full chain for a txn from its audit log. Who that team is and how to reach it is left to the organisation.
rows.rating_reason: Red: no contact field is defined (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Sharing txn with the agent's owning team.
claims.quote: a workload that observes unexpected behavior may share the `txn` claim and this value with the proximate agent's owning team

claims.text: The TTS operator can supply chain history.
claims.quote: A workload that shares the `txn` value with the TTS operator can obtain the full chain history

claims.text: Searched both drafts for contact, escalation, abuse and owner fields: No contact field.
claims.section: Searched both drafts for contact, escalation, abuse and owner fields

rows.answer: No. Neither draft defines a way for one service to warn others about a misbehaving agent. The extension recommends logging act, sub and agentic_ctx for behavioural monitoring and a persistent audit log at the Transaction Token Service, which support investigation after the fact inside the trust domain, but these are not signals between services.
rows.rating_reason: Red: not addressed (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Searched both drafts for signals, events, reputation and shared signals: No signals between services.
claims.section: Searched both drafts for signals, events, reputation and shared signals

claims.text: Monitoring through logging.
claims.quote: Systems SHOULD implement behavioral monitoring for AI agent activities by logging `act`, `sub`, and `agentic_ctx` claims in audit logs.

claims.text: TTS audit log.
claims.quote: The TTS SHOULD maintain a persistent audit log.

rows.answer: No. No claim names the AI model. Services needing provenance (e.g. software version identifiers) or attestation status SHOULD look them up in the Agent Attribute Store by agent identifier, but the store's interface is out of scope and model identity is not among the listed attributes.
rows.rating_reason: Red: nothing identifies the model (same as the three calibration examples).

claims.text: Provenance attributes listed for the store.
claims.quote: Provenance: Software version identifiers, manifest references, source code references.

claims.text: The store's interface is out of scope.
claims.section: 3.5.2. Agent Attribute Store Queries for Richer Context
claims.quote: The Agent Attribute Store interface, query protocol, and response format are out of scope for this specification.

claims.text: Searched both drafts for model, LLM version and provenance claims in the token: No model claim.
claims.section: Searched both drafts for model, LLM version and provenance claims in the token

goals_reading.access_control: Internal services get a narrow, required scope that can only shrink along the chain, the user (sub), the delegated agent (act) and, when agents are recognised, the originating and current agent and a hop count, so they can treat agent-driven calls differently from direct human calls.
goals_reading.incident_response: Nothing can be revoked in-band; tokens expire within minutes and new ones stop once the underlying access token is invalidated (if the service checks). Investigation is supported by the transaction ID and the Transaction Token Service's audit log.
goals_reading.accountability: An action inside the trust domain can be traced to the user, the agent that started the chain and the agent at the current hop (at application level), with the full chain reconstructable from the audit log; session identifiers are only self-asserted hints.

notes: The analysed text of the extension was taken from the author's GitHub repository at commit 5a40b0a (merged 31 October 2026, the -03 publication date). Its section structure was compared with the published -03 table of contents on the IETF datatracker. The source file's own heading numbers in Section 3 are offset by one from the published numbering (e.g. the file says 3.6 for what is published as 3.5 Agentic Context). Section labels in this report follow the published numbering. Quotes that cite sections (e.g. 'Section 3.4.1') keep the file's own numbers.

The base Transaction Tokens draft was taken from the oauth-wg repository at commit 146e47d, whose document history matches -11. Later edits on main (working-group last call feedback, August 2026) were not analysed.
RFC 9396 (Rich Authorization Requests) is listed as a normative reference in -03 but no longer used in its text.
Both drafts use RFC 2119 keywords; requirement levels are quoted as written. No instructions aimed at AI tools were found in the sources.
The IETF datatracker lists the base draft's working-group state as 'WG Consensus: Waiting for Write-Up' (seen 19 November 2026); this was not used as evidence in the report.
open_questions: Only the table of contents of the published -03 was compared with the repository text; small wording differences between the two cannot be ruled out.
How receiving workloads obtain the Transaction Token Service's signing keys is not specified (the base draft says the keys are 'often' known). This could affect validity in practice.
The agent instance identifier was rated yellow because session_id identifies the agent's runtime session; it could be argued red because the value is self-asserted and may not be used for decisions.

Whether the extension's MUST for mutually authenticated channels between all components lets a resource server link the calling workload to proximate_agent.id is not stated; authentication was rated red on that basis.
Credential lifetime was rated yellow because no verifier-enforced maximum exists; 'on the order of minutes' could be read as a specific short limit (green).

protocol.full_name: Trust Spanning Protocol (Trust over IP), with the TSP-Enabled AI Agent Protocols draft (TMCP, TA2A)
protocol.spec_version: TSP Release 1.0 (tswg-tsp-specification commit ccda6b3); TSP-Enabled AI Agent Protocols v1.0 Draft (GitHub Pages, accessed 2026-11-19)

summary: The Trust Spanning Protocol (TSP) is a general-purpose messaging layer from the Trust over IP Foundation, part of LF Decentralized Trust. It lets two parties that identify themselves with different kinds of verifiable identifiers (e.g. DIDs) exchange messages that are always authentic and, if wanted, confidential and private, much as IP connects different networks. Version 1.0 was approved by the Technology Stack Working Group on 30 October 2026. A separate ToIP draft, TSP-Enabled AI Agent Protocols, applies it to AI agents: TMCP runs MCP over TSP and TA2A runs A2A over TSP. That draft is incomplete, and TMCP exists mainly as an OpenWallet Foundation implementation.

Every TSP message names the sender's and receiver's identifiers (VIDs) and is signed with the sender's key, optionally encrypted to the receiver; the receiver resolves and appraises the sender's VID against its own policy before relying on it. TMCP wraps each MCP message in a TSP message over the normal MCP transport, and the draft makes each agent its own TSP endpoint, with authority delegated by signed credentials that can only narrow, must be revocable and must trace back to a person or organisation. TSP itself leaves out authorization, message freshness and trust decisions; the agent draft does not yet define the MCP binding, model identity, contact channels or warnings between services.
how_it_works: Setup: each agent or service (a TSP endpoint) controls one or more verifiable identifiers (VIDs), e.g. a did:webvh whose key history is published and supports key rotation. In the TMCP implementation, the MCP client and server each get their own DID.

Introduction: the client learns the server's VID out of band and sends a relationship-forming message (TSP_RFI). The server resolves the client's VID, verifies and appraises it against its own policy, and replies with TSP_RFA if it accepts.

Each message, e.g. an MCP JSON-RPC request in TMCP, is placed in a TSP message naming both VIDs, optionally encrypted to the receiver, and signed with the sender's key. It travels over the usual transport (Streamable HTTP, SSE, WebSockets) or through intermediaries.

The receiving endpoint checks that the relationship exists, verifies the signature against the sender's current key state, decrypts, checks that the sender VID inside matches, and passes the content up; anything that does not verify is silently dropped.

Under the draft agent companion, an agent exercising authority presents a chain of authorization credentials (ACDCs) from its principal. The receiver checks at that moment that every credential in the chain is valid and unrevoked and roots in an issuer it trusts, and computes the narrowed effective authority.
Afterwards, either side can cancel the relationship (TSP_RFD), a principal can revoke a delegation in its status registry, and a compromised key is rotated through the VID type.

rows.short: Signed messages between verifiable identifiers; agent draft adds delegation
rows.answer: A Trust over IP messaging layer where every message between two endpoints is signed, and optionally encrypted, under each side's verifiable identifier (e.g. a DID); a companion draft makes each AI agent its own endpoint with delegated, revocable authority, and TMCP/TA2A carry MCP and A2A messages inside TSP.

rows.short: Trust layer under MCP, A2A and other protocols
rows.answer: A general trust layer under higher-level protocols (agents, wallets, messaging), carried inside the message rather than in HTTP headers, so it works over HTTP, QUIC, queues or intermediaries. For agents, TMCP seals each MCP JSON-RPC message as a TSP message and sends it over the usual MCP transport, and TA2A does the same for A2A. The receiving endpoint verifies messages itself; intermediaries can route them but cannot forge them.

rows.short: Endpoints, Support Systems, Intermediaries; TEAs and principals

The agent draft adds the TSP-Enabled Agent (TEA), an agent that is itself a TSP endpoint, built around a Controller with a wallet and a TSP gateway, and principals (a natural person or organisation) who delegate authority to it.

rows.answer: A signature by the sender over every TSP message (envelope and payload), made with the key bound to the sender's VID, so it is proof of possession and covers the whole content. The payload can also be encrypted to the receiver, with the sender's VID inside. The signature binds the receiver's VID too, so a message cannot be redirected or disowned. In TMCP every MCP request, response and streamed event over Streamable HTTP is sealed this way.
rows.rating_reason: Green: a verifiable credential (signature) on every message (same as Web Bot Auth and Visa TAP, and stronger in that it covers the whole content).

Endpoints must not treat stale key state as current. The agent draft requires each delegated authority to carry a validUntil bound, but sets no maximum.

The receiving endpoint resolves the sender's VID through its VID type (e.g. a did:webvh history log), verifies that the sender controls it and appraises its records against its own policy, then checks the signature and the sender VID inside the payload. No prior relationship is needed beyond an introduction and a relationship-forming exchange. Messages are proven genuine and unaltered, but TSP has no timestamps, so whether a message is current or replayed is left to higher layers.

goals_reading.access_control: Core TSP lets a service accept or drop messages per sender VID and relationship, by its own policy. The draft adds delegation credentials whose narrowing authority a service can enforce, but the MCP binding that would map them to tool calls is not yet written.
goals_reading.incident_response: A service can cancel or block a relationship with one VID, which is one agent where each agent is its own endpoint. The draft adds per-delegation revocation checked at each use; key compromise is handled by VID rotation, which reaches each peer when it re-resolves.
goals_reading.accountability: Every message is signed and binds both sender and receiver VIDs, so the sender cannot disown it. The draft requires every authority to trace back to a natural person or organisation; the AI model and a contact are not identified.

notes: Both specifications use RFC 2119 keywords in capitals; requirement levels in this analysis follow them.

This analysis covers two documents. Rows rated from the TSP-Enabled AI Agent Protocols draft are marked coverage 'extension', because that draft is a separate, incomplete companion: its MCP over TSP, TEA Signed Payload and Security and Trust Considerations sections are TODO, and it has no A2A section.

The companion draft's GitHub repository showed no commits from this environment, so it was read only on its published GitHub Pages page; all quotes from it, and from the OWF book and LF Decentralized Trust blog, were checked with a web tool (WEB-OK).
TSP 1.0 was approved by the Technology Stack Working Group on 30 October 2026; the specification's foreword still has a placeholder for the Steering Committee approval date.

TMCP is described from the OpenWallet Foundation implementation (a transport hook on a fork of the MCP Python SDK). No public TA2A specification text or code was found; TA2A appears only in presentations and as a goal of the draft.
The rubric assumes a service receiving requests. TSP is a peer-to-peer messaging layer, so 'receiving service' is read as the receiving TSP endpoint (e.g. a TMCP server).
Venue is set to 'foundation' (Trust over IP, part of LF Decentralized Trust); the TSP specification is published under the OWF Contributor License and OWFa 1.0.
Name collision: an unrelated 'Trust Standard Protocol' (LexiTSP) for AI provenance also uses the abbreviation TSP. It was not used.
open_questions: Will the agent draft be updated to reference TSP 1.0 instead of TSP Rev 2, and do any of its requirements depend on Rev 2 behaviour?
How does TMCP interact with MCP's own OAuth-based authorization: does TSP replace it, or run underneath it? The draft's MCP binding is not written yet.
Is there any TA2A specification or implementation beyond presentation slides?
In practice, do deployments give each agent its own VID (as the draft intends) or share one VID across a provider's agents? This decides the identifier, instance and authentication ratings.
Who runs the credential status registries for delegation ACDCs, and how quickly do verifiers see a revocation?

protocol.name: UCP
protocol.full_name: Universal Commerce Protocol, with the Identity Linking capability
protocol.spec_version: UCP 2026-08-25 (release branch release/2026-08-25 at commit cfba1e7; tag v2026-08-25)
protocol.maintainer: UCP project (Governing Council with permanent seats for Google and Shopify, plus Domain Tech Councils); Apache 2.0
protocol.newer_version_note: 2026-08-25 is the latest release. The release branch received a backport (the ask capability) on 2026-11-02, which is included. The main branch has unreleased changes to identity-linking discovery (selection among several authorization servers) that were not analysed.

summary: The Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) is an open standard for how AI agents and other platforms shop with businesses: finding products, building carts, checking out, paying and managing orders. Its Identity Linking capability lets a platform act for a specific customer at a business by linking the customer's account there. Google and Shopify launched UCP in January 2026; it is run as an open-source project under Apache 2.0, with a Governing Council in which both hold permanent seats and Domain Tech Councils that include other large retailers and technology companies. The latest release, 2026-08-25, is used by Shopify and in Google's merchant integration.

Each business publishes a profile at /.well-known/ucp, and each platform names its own profile URL on every request in the UCP-Agent header. Businesses should authenticate platforms, for example with HTTP Message Signatures checked against keys in that profile, but API keys, OAuth or mTLS are also allowed. Identity Linking is standard OAuth with PKCE: the customer signs in and consents on the business's own authorization server, which issues a scoped bearer token, or a trusted identity provider vouches for the customer. Revoking a link must immediately invalidate its tokens. UCP does not identify individual agents or the AI model, sets no lifetime for request signatures, and defines no contact channel or warnings between businesses.
how_it_works: Setup: the business publishes its UCP profile at /.well-known/ucp (capabilities, endpoints, signing keys) and, if it offers Identity Linking, OAuth metadata and the scopes that need a signed-in customer. The platform publishes its own profile with its public keys.

On every request the platform sends its profile URL in the UCP-Agent header and, when it uses HTTP Message Signatures, signs the method, host, path, body digest, UCP-Agent and idempotency key with a key from that profile. Other authentication methods (API keys, OAuth client credentials, mTLS) are allowed instead.

The business fetches the platform profile, verifies the signature (or other credential), negotiates capabilities, and handles public or agent-authenticated operations such as browsing, carts and guest checkout.

For an operation gated by a scope, the business answers 401 identity_required. The platform runs OAuth with PKCE against the business's authorization server, where the customer signs in and consents, or, if the business trusts an identity provider the platform already holds a token for, obtains a 60-second JWT grant from that provider and exchanges it at the business.

The platform then sends the business-issued token as a bearer token. The business validates issuer, audience, expiry, scopes and client, and decides; checkout can still require the buyer's own review through a handoff link, and the AP2 extension can require signed purchase mandates.
When the customer unlinks, the platform must revoke the token at the business, and the business must reject it from then on; a compromised platform key is removed from the platform's profile.

rows.short: Agentic commerce standard with OAuth account linking
rows.answer: An open commerce standard, launched by Google and Shopify, where shopping agents and other platforms name a published profile on every request (optionally signing it), and use OAuth Identity Linking to act for a signed-in customer at a business with scoped, revocable tokens.

claims.text: Purpose of Identity Linking.
claims.quote: The Identity Linking capability enables a platform to obtain authorization to perform actions on behalf of a user on a business's (relying party) site.

claims.text: Platforms name their profile on every request.
claims.quote: Platforms MUST communicate their profile URI with each request to enable capability negotiation.

rows.short: Agentic shopping: catalog, cart, checkout, orders
rows.answer: Commerce between platforms (AI agents, apps, websites acting for a buyer) and businesses: catalog search, carts, checkout, payment and orders, with newer domains such as lodging and food. Requests travel over REST, MCP, A2A or an embedded protocol; identity sits in HTTP headers (UCP-Agent, signatures, bearer tokens) and some data in the body (buyer, signals, AP2 mandates). The business verifies them itself; Web Bot Auth-shaped signatures can also be checked by bot-management layers.

claims.text: Who the platform is.
claims.quote: The consumer-facing surface (AI agent, app, website) acting on behalf of the user to discover businesses and facilitate commerce.

claims.text: What identity linking unlocks.
claims.quote: accessing loyalty benefits, personalized offers, saved addresses, wishlists, and order history.

claims.text: Optional Web Bot Auth interop.
claims.quote: Signers opting into WBA-shape signatures additionally emit a Signature-Agent header advertising their keys.

rows.short: Platform, Business, User; PSP, Credential Provider, IdP
rows.answer: Identity Linking names three participants. Platform: the trusted intermediary that links identity and presents user identity tokens. Business: hosts its own OAuth authorization server, authenticates users and issues tokens. User: the person whose identity is linked. The wider spec adds the Payment Service Provider (processes payments for the business), the Credential Provider (e.g. a wallet holding the user's credentials) and, optionally, external identity providers that the business trusts.

summary: Verifiable Intent (VI) gives merchants and payment networks signed proof of what a user allowed an AI shopping agent to buy, and that the agent stayed within it. It addresses a gap in agentic commerce: today's payment systems assume a person is present at checkout, so nobody can check whether an agent's purchase matches the user's wishes. Mastercard publishes and maintains it, co-developed with Google and aligned with Google's AP2 and UCP. It is an open draft (v0.1) under Apache 2.0, with a Python reference SDK; Mastercard has announced plans to integrate it into its Agent Pay APIs.

VI is a credential format, not a transport: it rides inside other commerce protocols. It chains three layers of selective-disclosure JWTs (SD-JWT). A card issuer signs a long-lived credential binding the user's key; the user signs a mandate with either the final cart and payment (Immediate mode) or limits such as amount, merchants and products plus the agent's key (Autonomous mode); in Autonomous mode the agent signs short-lived final values for the merchant and the payment network. Each party sees only its part. VI leaves out revocation (deferred), transport, agent key provisioning, contact channels, cross-party signalling and model identity.
how_it_works: Setup: the user registers a public key with a card issuer (a bank or payment network such as Mastercard), which signs a Layer 1 (L1) credential binding that key to an opaque user identifier and card details. It sits in a Credential Provider's wallet and lasts about a year.

When the user asks an agent to buy something, the user (or a wallet holding the user's key) signs a Layer 2 (L2) credential: either the final cart and payment values (Immediate mode, valid about 15 minutes) or constraints such as amount range, allowed merchants and products, plus the agent's public key (Autonomous mode, typically 24 hours to 30 days).

In Autonomous mode the agent picks the products, obtains the checkout contents and signs two Layer 3 (L3) credentials with its own key, valid about 5 minutes and at most 1 hour: L3b with the checkout for the merchant and L3a with the payment for the payment network, linked by a shared hash.

The agent hands the chain to the merchant and the payment network inside whatever commerce protocol is in use, disclosing only the checkout parts to the merchant and only the payment parts to the network.

The merchant verifies the issuer's signature on L1 using the issuer's published keys, the user's signature on L2, the agent's signature on L3b (in Autonomous mode), the hash links and expiry times, and checks the checkout against the disclosed constraints and its own records.

The payment network does the same for the payment side, checks payment constraints, enforces one purchase per mandate and tracks cumulative spend, then routes the authorization; the issuer makes the final decision.

Agent: AI software acting for the user, which signs Layer 3 in Autonomous mode. Merchant: sells the goods, creates checkouts and verifies. Payment Network: routes and settles payments and verifies the chain before authorization. Verifier: any party that validates the chain.

rows.short: SD-JWT (RFC 9901), JWS, JWK, ES256, RFC 7800 cnf
rows.answer: Selective Disclosure JWT (SD-JWT, RFC 9901) as the base format, with JWS (RFC 7515), JWK (RFC 7517), JWT (RFC 7519) and ES256 from JWA (RFC 7518) as the only required algorithm. The cnf confirmation claim (RFC 7800) binds each layer's key to the next. SHA-256 and base64url (RFC 4648) are used for hashes. Token Status List (RFC 9701) is only mentioned as a possible future revocation mechanism. VI positions itself as a concrete credential format for AP2's verifiable digital credentials.

claims.quote: Base credential format; provides selective disclosure of claims via salted hash commitments

claims.text: ES256 is required.
claims.quote: Implementations MUST support ES256 (ECDSA using the P-256 curve and SHA-256) as defined in [RFC 7518] Section 3.4.

rows.short: Platform URL; agent key ID in Autonomous mode
rows.answer: Partly. The user's Layer 2 carries an audience (aud) that identifies the agent, typically the agent platform's URL, and is always visible. In Autonomous mode the user also binds the agent's public key with a key identifier (kid), and each Layer 3 carries that kid in its header, so the merchant can tell which delegated agent key signed. In Immediate mode there is no agent key, only the platform audience.

rows.short: Per-delegation agent key, Autonomous mode only
rows.answer: Partly. In Autonomous mode, the merchant sees the kid of the agent key that the user bound for this delegation, and the security model recommends that platforms generate a fresh key pair per delegation session, so the key can single out one delegated agent. The dispute evidence table says the agent key signature shows the specific agent that executed the transaction. This exists only in Autonomous mode, and fresh keys are a recommendation.

claims.quote: VI binds an agent key via the L2 mandate's cnf.jwk but does not specify how that key is generated, communicated to the user's L2 construction environment, or stored.

rows.answer: Yes. Every chain starts with the Layer 1 credential, which the merchant must verify, and which always shows an opaque, stable user identifier (sub) assigned by the issuer, plus the card's last four digits and scheme. The user's email is selectively disclosable and shown only when needed. Layer 2 is signed with the user's key bound in Layer 1, so the merchant learns which issuer-known user authorized the purchase, though only through a pseudonymous identifier.
rows.rating_reason: Green: the protocol requires an issuer-signed user identifier in the root credential that the merchant receives and verifies (unlike Visa TAP's optional consumer object).

rows.answer: Partly, per purchase rather than per request. The merchant receives a chain of SD-JWTs signed with ES256: the issuer's Layer 1, the user's key-bound Layer 2 and, in Autonomous mode, the agent's Layer 3b. Each later layer is signed with the key named in the previous one, which is proof of possession, and carries a nonce, an audience, issue and expiry times and a hash of the layer below. VI defines no transport, so it is presented with the purchase, not on every HTTP request.
rows.rating_reason: Yellow: a strong, verifiable credential, but defined only for the purchase presentation and not for every request to the merchant (transport is out of scope); borderline green.

claims.text: Key binding through each layer.
claims.quote: Each layer cryptographically binds the next layer's signing authority through the cnf (confirmation) claim defined in [RFC 7800].

claims.quote: Cryptographically random nonce. MUST be distinct from the L2 nonce.
