claims.quote: Out of scope: Transport protocols, key management/provisioning, credential provider enrollment, agent platform APIs, dispute resolution, regulatory compliance mapping (PCI DSS, PSD2, etc.).

rows.short: Agent layer max 1 hour; delegation up to 30 days
rows.answer: Partly. The agent's Layer 3 must not exceed 1 hour (5 minutes recommended), and an Immediate-mode Layer 2 should last no more than 15 minutes. Verifiers must reject any layer whose expiry has passed (with about 300 seconds of clock skew). However, the user's Autonomous delegation (Layer 2) may last up to 30 days or longer, up to the Layer 1 expiry of about a year, and verifiers are not told to reject Layer 3 credentials issued with a window longer than 1 hour.

rows.answer: Yes. The merchant fetches the issuer's public key from its published key set (JWKS) using the kid, verifies the Layer 1 signature, then verifies Layer 2 with the user key inside Layer 1 and Layer 3 with the agent key inside Layer 2, checks the hash links, the typ header of each layer and the expiry times. No prior relationship with the agent is needed; the merchant only needs the issuer's keys.

The merchant itself verifies proof from individual keys: in Autonomous mode, Layer 3b signed by the agent key that the user bound for this delegation; in both modes, Layer 2 signed by the user's key that the issuer bound. But VI binds keys, not people: the user's key may be held by a platform on the user's behalf, which verifiers cannot tell apart, and whether each agent gets its own key is only recommended.

rows.answer: Yes. In Autonomous mode, the user's signed Layer 2 carries typed constraints: allowed merchants, line items, allowed payees, amount range, total budget, recurrence and a checkout-payment reference. Verifiers must check the agent's final values against the disclosed constraints; the merchant checks the checkout side and the payment network the payment side, including cumulative budgets. In Immediate mode the user signs the final cart and amount directly. Unknown constraint types are skipped by default (permissive mode).
rows.rating_reason: Green: the credential carries fine-grained, user-signed limits that verifiers must enforce (same colour as MCP Authorization's scopes).

rows.answer: Yes. Every purchase rests on a Layer 2 that the user signs: in Immediate mode the user reviews and confirms the final cart and payment, and in Autonomous mode the user signs the limits and the agent's key before the agent can act. rows.short: Card issuer vouches for user; user for agent
rows.answer: The card issuer and the user. The issuer, called a trusted third party, signs Layer 1 to vouch for the user and the user's key; the user then vouches for the agent by binding its key in a signed mandate. Only agents a verified user has delegated to can produce a valid chain. Nobody vets the agent platform itself, and VI does not say how a merchant decides which issuers to accept.

rows.short: Not defined in v0.1; short lifetimes
rows.answer: Not defined. Version 0.1 has no credential revocation; the specification lists it as a known limitation and names Token Status List as a candidate. Meanwhile, short lifetimes limit exposure, an issuer can remove a compromised signing key from its JWKS (which invalidates every Layer 1 signed with it), and issuers keep their usual card-level blocks. A single delegation cannot be revoked before it expires, so an Autonomous mandate can stay usable for weeks.

goals_reading.access_control: The merchant can check that a purchase was authorized by an issuer-known user and stays within user-signed limits (merchants, items, amounts), and the payment network enforces payment limits and budgets. VI does not control access to the merchant's other endpoints.
goals_reading.incident_response: There is no revocation in v0.1; short agent credentials and mandate expiry limit damage, an issuer can pull a signing key (affecting all its credentials) or block the card. A single delegation cannot be cut off early, and there is no contact channel.
goals_reading.accountability: The chain gives signed evidence linking the issuer, a pseudonymous user, the user's exact instructions and, in Autonomous mode, the agent key that executed, which any party can verify in a dispute. It identifies the agent platform only by URL and not the model.

summary: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol (TAP) helps online merchants tell AI shopping agents that Visa has approved apart from other bots. As agents begin to browse shops and pay on behalf of consumers, merchants need a way to let approved agents through while still blocking other automated traffic. TAP is a vendor specification published by Visa in October 2025, developed with Cloudflare, and available on the Visa Developer Center and GitHub under Visa's terms of use.

An approved agent provider signs each request to a merchant with HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), the same building block as Web Bot Auth, and marks it as browsing or paying. The merchant, or a CDN in front of it, checks the signature against public keys that Visa publishes, a validity window of at most 8 minutes, and a one-time nonce. A request may also carry signed objects describing the consumer (an ID token with a stable identifier and obfuscated contact details) and the payment. TAP does not identify the individual agent, and leaves spending limits, purchase approval (handled by Visa Intelligent Commerce) and revocation outside the protocol.
how_it_works: An agent provider is onboarded with Visa, and its public keys are published in Visa's key store at a well-known location.

When the agent contacts a merchant, it signs the request with an HTTP Message Signature that includes created and expires times, a keyid, a nonce and a tag: agent-browser-auth for browsing or agent-payer-auth for paying.

The request may also carry an Agentic Consumer Recognition Object (information about the consumer) and payment information in an Agentic Payment Container, each signed with the same key and linked by the same nonce.

The merchant, or a site protection provider in front of it (e.g. a CDN), retrieves Visa's public key and checks the signature, the time window of at most 8 minutes and that the nonce has not been seen before. If any check does not pass, the message should be blocked.

If the checks pass, the merchant treats the request as coming from an approved agent and can use the consumer information to recognise its customer. Payment approval and limits are handled by Visa outside TAP.

summary: Web Bot Auth is a way for bots and AI agents to prove, on every web request, which operator's key signed it. It is aimed at automated traffic on the open web (e.g. AI assistants, search indexing, content aggregation and automated testing), where websites today rely on IP address lists and User-Agent strings that are hard to manage or easy to fake. It is an Internet-Draft of the IETF Web Bot Auth working group, at revision -00 (September 2026). It has public implementations but is not yet an RFC.

The agent's operator publishes its public keys in a key directory at an HTTPS URL. The agent names that URL in a Signature-Agent header and signs each request with HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), covering at least the target host and a validity window. A website, or a CDN in front of it, fetches the key and checks the signature without any prior relationship with the agent, and can then allow, rate-limit or block that operator. The draft deliberately leaves out who the user is, what the agent may do, whether the operator should be trusted, and how to revoke keys.
how_it_works: The agent's operator creates a signing key and publishes the public key in a JSON key directory (JWKS), by default at a well-known URL on its own domain.

For each request, the agent adds a Signature-Agent header naming that directory and signs the request with an HTTP Message Signature covering the target host, with created and expires times, a keyid and the tag web-bot-auth.
The website, or a proxy or CDN in front of it, reads the signature headers and, if it does not already have the key, fetches it from the Signature-Agent URL.
It verifies the signature and checks that the current time is inside the signature's validity window.
It applies its own policy to the identified operator, e.g. allow, rate-limit or block.

summary: WIMSE (Workload Identity in Multi System Environments) is an IETF working group defining how software workloads, such as microservices, jobs or AI agents running as services, prove who they are when they call each other. This analysis covers two of its drafts together: the Workload Credentials draft, which defines the Workload Identity Token (WIT) and the Workload Identity Certificate (WIC), and the Workload Proof Token (WPT) draft, which proves possession of the key in a WIT on each HTTP request. Both are working-group drafts (workload-creds-03, October 2026; wpt-02, August 2026), with early implementations listed for SPIFFE, Defakto Security and Teleport.

An Identity Server in a trust domain issues each workload a short-lived WIT, a signed JWT naming its Workload Identifier (a URI) and binding a public key. On each call, the workload sends the WIT plus a WPT signed with its own key, bound to the target URI, the WIT and any user-context tokens, valid for minutes or seconds. The receiving workload checks both against trust anchors configured for that trust domain, then authorizes by the identifier. The drafts leave out authorization rules, user identity (carried in separate tokens such as Txn-Tokens), revocation (short lifetimes instead), contact channels, cross-party signalling and model identity.
how_it_works: Setup: each trust domain runs an Identity Server; receiving workloads are configured, out of band, with which issuers and trust anchors (e.g. a JWKS or a certification authority) belong to which trust domain.

The Identity Server issues workload A a Workload Identity Token: a JWT naming its Workload Identifier in sub, an expiry (typically hours) and, in cnf, the public key whose private half workload A holds. (For mutual TLS, it can instead hold a Workload Identity Certificate.)

When workload A calls workload B over TLS, it sends the WIT in the Workload-Identity-Token header and a Workload Proof Token in the Authorization header with the WPT scheme. The WPT is a JWT signed with workload A's key, carrying the target URI as audience, a short expiry, a unique jti, a hash of the WIT and hashes of any user-context tokens such as a Txn-Token.

Workload B validates the WIT against the trust anchors for the trust domain in its sub, then checks the WPT: signature with the WIT's key and algorithm, audience against its own configured URI, expiry, WIT hash, token hashes and, as recommended, that the jti is new.
Workload B then authorizes the call under its own policy using the authenticated Workload Identifier (e.g. matching it against access lists) and logs it; the drafts define no permissions format.

protocol.name: x402
protocol.spec_version: Protocol Version 2 (x402-specification-v2.md, version history entry v2.0 of 2025-12-09) with the v2 HTTP and MCP transports, the exact scheme and the official extensions, read at commit b007387 of x402-foundation/x402
protocol.spec_date: v2 released 2025-12-11; text read at commit b007387 dated 2026-11-18
protocol.maintainer: x402 Foundation (Linux Foundation), created by Coinbase
protocol.newer_version_note: Protocol version 2 is the latest; no version 3 exists in the repository. The v2 specification text has kept being edited without a version change (latest edit to the core file on 2026-10-26), so the analysis is pinned to commit b007387. Version 1 remains in the repository and the reference SDKs stay backward-compatible with it.

summary: x402 lets a client, typically an AI agent or an app, pay for an API call, a web page or an MCP tool inside the request itself, using the long-unused HTTP status 402 Payment Required. It is aimed at services that want to charge per use without accounts, API keys or card checkouts. Coinbase created it in 2025; since 2026 it is governed by the x402 Foundation under the Linux Foundation, with about 40 member organisations. Protocol version 2 was released in December 2025 and Coinbase runs a hosted production facilitator; most payments use stablecoins on blockchains.

A server answers an unpaid request with its payment requirements (amount, asset, network, recipient, time limit). The client signs a payment authorization with its wallet key and retries with it in a header (or in MCP or A2A metadata). The server, usually through a facilitator service, checks the signature, balance, amount and validity window, runs the request and settles the payment on chain. x402 proves that someone with a funded wallet paid, not who the agent is or for whom it acts: identity comes only from optional extensions (wallet sign-in, HTTP Message Signatures or OAuth hints). It defines no scopes, human approval, revocation, contact channel or model identity.
how_it_works: Setup: the resource server picks a facilitator (e.g. Coinbase's hosted one, or its own) and a recipient wallet; the client holds a wallet with funds on a supported network. No account or prior relationship between them is needed.

The client (e.g. an AI agent) requests a resource. The server replies 402 Payment Required with a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header listing accepted payment options: scheme (e.g. exact), network, amount, asset, recipient (payTo) and maxTimeoutSeconds.

The client chooses an option, signs a payment authorization with its wallet key (for exact on EVM: an EIP-3009 transfer authorization from its address to payTo, with a validity window and a random nonce) and retries the request with it in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header.

The server sends the payload to the facilitator's /verify endpoint, which checks the signature recovers to the payer, the balance, the amount, recipient and validity window, and simulates the transfer.

If valid, the server runs the request, then calls /settle; the facilitator submits the transfer on chain. The server returns the result with a PAYMENT-RESPONSE header carrying the transaction and the payer's address. (Some schemes settle before the request runs.)

rows.short: Pay per request over HTTP 402 with signed wallet payments
rows.answer: An open payment protocol where a server answers 402 Payment Required with its price and a client, such as an AI agent, retries with a payment authorization signed by its wallet, which the server verifies and settles (usually through a facilitator) before or after serving the request.

rows.answer: Pay-per-use access to APIs, content and AI tools, including agents paying autonomously. On HTTP, the requirements travel in a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header on a 402 response and the payment in a PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header; on MCP and A2A, in message metadata. The resource server decides, usually by calling a facilitator that verifies and settles the payment; servers can also host those endpoints themselves.

goals_reading.access_control: A server can gate each resource behind a verified payment of a set amount, so access follows payment; it learns a payer wallet address but not the agent's identity, principal or permissions unless optional extensions are used.
goals_reading.incident_response: A server can refuse further payments from a wallet address, but anyone can create a new wallet; there is no revocation, contact channel or way to warn other servers.
goals_reading.accountability: Each paid request can be traced to a wallet address and an on-chain transaction, which is durable and public, but linking that wallet to an agent, operator or user requires information outside the core protocol.

notes: Name collision: 'x402' refers to this payment protocol; it is unrelated to the X.400/X.509 ITU-T standards naming. Version 1 and version 2 of x402 differ (e.g. v1 used X-PAYMENT headers); this analysis covers version 2.

Mechanism profile is 'other': the per-request proof is a blockchain payment authorization signed with a wallet key (e.g. EIP-712/EIP-3009), which none of the fixed mechanism values describes. HTTP Message Signatures appear only in an optional extension.

The x402 specification mixes RFC 2119 capitals (MUST, SHOULD) with lowercase 'must' and table 'Required' markers. Requirement tags with an asterisk reflect points that rest on schema 'Required' fields or lowercase words.
Extensions (sign-in-with-x, http-message-signatures, auth-hints, payment-identifier) are published in the same repository and rated as 'extension' coverage.

The x402.org, Linux Foundation and Coinbase pages were checked with a web tool, which limits quotes to about 125 characters, so some quotes are fragments. An earlier Coinbase FAQ sentence about operating 'the first production facilitator' was no longer on the page and was not used.
first_published 2025-05 reflects Coinbase's announcement of x402 in May 2025 as reported by secondary sources; it is not cited in the rows.
open_questions: How strictly do facilitators bound the EVM validBefore value relative to maxTimeoutSeconds, given that the EVM verification step only says the window must 'meet' the requirements?
Which servers use the sign-in-with-x or HTTP Message Signatures extensions in production to identify agents?
